title: Robin đen được người dân New Zealand bình chọn 'chú chim của năm'
content:
Cuộc bình chọn thu hút số người tham gia kỷ lục
Ngày 21-9, báo The Guardian đưa tin chim robin đen (black robin, tên khoa học Petroica traversi) vừa được bình chọn là "Chim của năm" tại New Zealand. Đây từng được coi là loài chim quý hiếm nhất thế giới, trước khi một dự án bảo tồn phi thường cứu chúng khỏi bờ vực tuyệt chủng.
Loài chim nhỏ này chỉ sinh sống trên quần đảo Chatham, cách đảo chính New Zealand khoảng 800km về phía đông.
Cuộc bình chọn "Chim của năm" do Tổ chức bảo tồn Forest & Bird (New Zealand) tổ chức, được khởi động cách đây 20 năm nhằm nâng cao nhận thức về tình trạng của các loài chim bản địa tại New Zealand.
Nhiều loài trong số này đang bị đe dọa, đứng trước nguy cơ tuyệt chủng hoặc đã tuyệt chủng do các loài gây hại du nhập, hoạt động của con người và môi trường sống ngày càng thu hẹp.
Cuộc bình chọn năm 2026 thu hút số phiếu kỷ lục 105.000 phiếu. Khoảng 88% số phiếu đến từ New Zealand.
Kākāpō (loài vẹt nặng nhất thế giới) đứng thứ hai, trong khi kārearea (loài chim ưng duy nhất của New Zealand và là quán quân năm 2025) xếp thứ ba năm nay.
Trong nhiều năm qua, cuộc bình chọn từng vướng không ít vụ việc gây tranh cãi, từ việc một con dơi giành chiến thắng năm 2021, đến cáo buộc Nga can thiệp vào cuộc bình chọn năm 2019 và cáo buộc người Úc tìm cách thao túng cuộc bình chọn năm 2018 để giúp loài chim cốc (shag) chiến thắng.
Năm 2023, người dẫn chương trình tin tức hài mang hai quốc tịch Anh - Mỹ John Oliver đã phát động chiến dịch toàn cầu ủng hộ pūteketeke, loài chim đang bị đe dọa. Loài chim này sau đó giành chiến thắng trong cuộc bình chọn cùng năm.
Chim robin đen có gì đặc biệt?
Chim robin đen có bộ lông đen nổi bật, đôi mắt đen và chiếc mỏ nhọn cũng màu đen.
Trong tiếng Māori, loài này được gọi là "kakaruia", còn trong tiếng Moriori (ngôn ngữ của người bản địa trên quần đảo Chatham) là "karure".
Sự suy giảm môi trường sống cùng các loài gây hại du nhập đã đẩy quần thể chim robin đen đến bờ vực tuyệt chủng. Đến thập niên 1970 chỉ còn 5 con, trong đó chỉ còn một cặp có khả năng sinh sản.
Sau đó, một chương trình nhân giống tiên phong sử dụng các loài chim khác để ấp và nuôi hộ trứng robin đen đã đạt được thành công, giúp số lượng loài này tăng dần lên 350 con trưởng thành, dù chúng vẫn được xếp vào nhóm "bị đe dọa".
New Zealand rất đặc biệt về mặt tiến hóa, nhất là với các loài chim. Lịch sử cô lập về địa lý kéo dài góp phần tạo nên một hệ chim độc đáo, với nhiều loài và cả những nhánh tiến hóa không có ở nơi nào khác trên thế giới.
Vì vậy, khi một loài chim đặc hữu tuyệt chủng, mất mát không chỉ dừng lại ở một loài mà trong một số trường hợp còn có thể đồng nghĩa với mất đi cả một nhánh trên "cây tiến hóa" đã hình thành qua hàng triệu năm.

title: Alberi per trattenere l’azoto e tecniche di semina intelligenti: così gli agricoltori della Tanzania si stanno adattando alle precipitazioni imprevedibili
content:
Alberi per trattenere l’azoto e tecniche di semina intelligenti: così gli agricoltori della Tanzania si stanno adattando alle precipitazioni imprevedibili
Indice
A Udumka la risposta alle piogge che arrivano male, troppo forti o tutte insieme sta crescendo dentro un vivaio. La comunità del sud della Tanzania ha cominciato a coltivare specie capaci di trattenere acqua e fissare l’azoto, inserendole in terreni messi alla prova dalle coltivazioni intensive e dalle precipitazioni che possono trascinare via i nutrienti. Nessuna tecnologia futuriatica. Qui si piantano alberi.
Il vivaio è gestito dall’Udumka Environmental Group, collettivo locale coinvolto nel progetto Her Resilience, Our Planet. La scelta delle specie serve a recuperare gradualmente fertilità e a rendere i campi meno fragili davanti a un clima diventato più irregolare. A lavorarci ci sono anche formatori scelti e preparati all’interno della comunità, così le conoscenze non rimangono appese all’arrivo di tecnici esterni. È uno degli interventi raccontati da CARE Tanzania, che partecipa al progetto.
Gli alberi entrano nei campi
Gli alberi azotofissatori lavorano soprattutto sottoterra. Grazie alla relazione con alcuni batteri presenti nelle radici, contribuiscono a rendere disponibile nel sistema agricolo l’azoto atmosferico, uno dei nutrienti essenziali per le piante. Nel tempo entrano in gioco anche foglie, radici e materia organica lasciata sul terreno.
È un principio usato da tempo nei sistemi agroforestali e documentato anche dalla FAO: alberi e colture possono condividere lo stesso spazio agricolo, con effetti sulla fertilità del terreno, sulla gestione dell’acqua e sulla protezione del suolo. A Udumka questa vecchia idea agricola viene rimessa al lavoro dentro un problema molto contemporaneo.
Le piogge, infatti, sono diventate più difficili da prevedere. CARE descrive precipitazioni violente, grandine e allagamenti capaci di compromettere i raccolti e impoverire ulteriormente terreni già sfruttati. Piantare una specie adatta, qui, significa cercare di lasciare qualcosa nel terreno anche quando l’acqua porta via il resto.
A pochi chilometri, cambiano anche le patate
Nel vicino villaggio di Kihesa Mgagao, Bariki Kagine coltivava patate con risultati scarsi e raccolti particolarmente vulnerabili alla grandine. Poi ha cominciato a cambiare diverse cose insieme: la distanza tra le piante, il momento della semina, l’uso delle previsioni meteorologiche, la fertilizzazione, la gestione dei parassiti e perfino la varietà coltivata. Ha scelto la Sagitta, più adatta al suo terreno. Il raccolto ottenuto gli ha fruttato circa 2 milioni di scellini tanzaniani, secondo quanto riportato da CARE.
È il risultato di un solo agricoltore, ma il cambiamento si vede bene: spostare una semina, lasciare più spazio tra le piante, scegliere una varietà diversa può fare la differenza quando il calendario delle piogge smette di comportarsi come prima. E infatti l’adattamento, da queste parti, ha un aspetto piuttosto poco spettacolare. Un albero nel posto giusto. Una patata piantata qualche giorno dopo. Un agricoltore che guarda le previsioni prima di entrare nel campo.
Il progetto punta a coinvolgere oltre 60 mila piccoli agricoltori
Her Resilience, Our Planet lavora nel bacino del Great Ruaha River, una delle aree agricole e naturali più importanti della Tanzania meridionale. Il programma è sostenuto anche da Global Affairs Canada e, secondo la scheda ufficiale del Governo canadese, proseguirà fino al 2030. CARE indica tra gli obiettivi oltre 60.000 piccoli agricoltori e 18.000 imprenditori agricoli coinvolti nella regione, con particolare attenzione a donne e giovani. Sono traguardi previsti dal progetto, non persone già raggiunte.
Per ora la storia è molto più piccola, ed è probabilmente per questo che funziona. Un vivaio gestito dal villaggio. Alberi scelti anche per ciò che fanno al terreno. Un agricoltore che cambia il modo di coltivare le patate e riesce a venderle meglio. Da Udumka non arriva una soluzione pronta per qualsiasi campo africano. Arriva qualcosa di più concreto: mentre il clima cambia le regole, questa comunità sta cambiando il modo di stare sul terreno. A volte cominciando da un albero.

- Nei villaggi della Tanzania la crisi climatica si combatte con alveari, pollai e donne finalmente ammesse alle decisioni
- La crisi climatica si manifesta in modo differente in ciascun Paese: la campagna globale del clima nata dal basso e diffusa via Whatsapp
- In Burkina Faso hanno lasciato decidere alle donne come spendere i soldi per il clima: ora usano il 30% di legna in meno

title: Looking back to look ahead: a BERTopic-assisted scoping review of Medical Humanities (2000-2025).
content: This study provides a scoping review of the periodical BMJ Medical Humanities in order to identify thematic changes evident in the journal between 2000 to 2025. Metadata for the review, including abstracts, publication years, authors and PubMed Identifiers (PMIDs), were gathered from PubMed, followed by data cleaning to remove partial and duplicate documents; the resulting final corpus consisted of 912 open access validated sources. Analysis was conducted in three parts: (1) Prevalent topics were identified using BERTopic, a topic-modelling approach based on transformers well suited to large corpora; (2) Themes were created using a synthesis of machine-derived topics; and (3) Data were visualised through R to identify changes in the themes. Five overarching themes emerged from the analysis: The Patient Journeys & Specific Conditions has grown significantly since 2015, indicating a growing interest in the journal towards articles addressing phenomenology, stigma, disabilities and personal experiences. Meanwhile, Narrative & Arts in Health and History & Culture of Medicine have remained foundational while Practice & Education and Mind, Body & Ethics remain reflective themes. This paper highlights the debate between narrative medicine and narrative humility and the importance of critical and posthumanist perspectives, thereby promoting structural and phenomenological research approaches. The study's findings may be limited by its use of abstracts only in topic modelling and the sensitivity of machine learning parameters. The study concludes with a discussion on its findings' implications for justice-based education in the medical humanities and mixed-methods syntheses in the field.

title: Rural Cancer Care Delivery in the United States: A 2026 Update on Disparities, Vulnerable Populations, and Emerging Models.
content: Rural Americans with cancer face persistent and widening disparities in incidence, stage at diagnosis, treatment access, and mortality. This paper synthesizes evidence on the financial sustainability of rural oncology programs, the populations bearing the greatest burden of rural cancer disparities, and the care delivery models most likely to narrow those gaps. We conducted a narrative review of English-language literature published through early 2026, drawing from peer-reviewed articles, national surveillance data, ASCO abstracts, and policy analyses. Rural oncology programs face significant financial challenges: 85% of rural hospitals are strained or vulnerable, cancer services at critical access hospitals (CAHs) have declined, and the 340B Drug Pricing Program's orphan-drug exclusion for CAHs represents an underappreciated structural gap that undermines program sustainability for the facilities most dependent on it. Rural-urban cancer mortality gaps are widest among adults younger than 65 years (the age paradox), who lack Medicare's partial safety net. Racial and ethnic minorities in rural areas, particularly Black Americans and American Indian/Alaska Natives, face compounding geographic and structural barriers. Counter to longstanding assumptions, the per-capita supply of rural oncologists grew approximately 20% nationally from 2012 to 2022, with 67% growth in the most isolated areas. Several models show promise, including hub-and-spoke networks, teleoncology, Project Extension for Community Healthcare Outcomes (ECHO) telementoring, CAH-based programs, patient navigation, oncology hospital-at-home, and National Cancer Institute Community Oncology Research Program (NCORP) sites. However, a key paradox persists: regions with the poorest geographic access to cancer centers have the lowest telehealth utilization rates. Rural cancer disparities are fundamentally a policy and equity problem, not a technology or geography problem. Proven delivery models exist, but they require concurrent policy investment to realize their full potential. Closing the gap requires permanent telehealth authorization, with payment parity, Medicaid expansion, advanced practice provider workforce investment, targeted 340B reform for CAHs, and interstate licensure reform. Oncologists and health systems have both the evidence and the ethical obligation to advocate for these changes, including through participation in hub-and-spoke affiliate networks, NCORP sites, or ECHO programs in their own communities.

title: Fibre Excellence : l’Etat dénonce « l’incurie » du liquidateur et reprend en main la sécurité de l’usine de pâte à papier de Tarascon
content:
L’Etat a annoncé vendredi 18 septembre reprendre en main la mise en sécurité de l’usine de pâte à papier Fibre Excellence de Tarascon (Bouches-du-Rhône), en cessation d’activité, pour pallier « l’incurie et les mises en danger réitérées de l’environnement » du liquidateur judiciaire.
« Face à la défaillance des liquidateurs de Fibre excellence et au vu de la situation du site de Tarascon, classé Seveso, l’Etat a décidé de faire intervenir l’Ademe [Agence de l’environnement et de la maîtrise de l’énergie] en urgence impérieuse afin de prévenir les risques d’incendie, de déversement de produits dangereux et de pollution du Rhône », précise un communiqué du ministère chargé de la transition écologique.
Le communiqué rappelle que depuis l’arrêt de l’activité, « d’importants volumes de bois et de produits chimiques demeurent stockés à proximité immédiate du Rhône ». Une récente visite des services de l’Etat a mis en évidence « la présence de bois, de produits dangereux et de déchets répartis sur l’ensemble du site, dont des déchets dangereux liquides ». L’intervention de l’Etat est ainsi justifiée par une « situation d’urgence impérieuse ».
La facture adressée aux liquidateurs
L’usine de Tarascon, qui employait 270 personnes, a été placée en liquidation judiciaire le 29 juillet. Depuis début septembre, la mise en sécurité de ce site classé « Seveso seuil bas » est au cœur d’un bras de fer entre le liquidateur judiciaire, la préfecture et les anciens salariés. La préfecture des Bouches-du-Rhône a mis en demeure le liquidateur de prendre des mesures pour prévenir tout risque de pollution. Mais « depuis des semaines, l’incurie des liquidateurs fait obstacle à la mise en œuvre des arrêtés » préfectoraux, note Mathieu Lefèvre, ministre délégué chargé de la transition écologique, cité dans le communiqué.
Au nom de la mise en sécurité du site, une dizaine d’anciens salariés désormais licenciés ainsi que des soutiens externes ont pénétré jeudi soir sur le site de 46 hectares pour relancer les pompes et la station d’épuration. « On est satisfaits, c’est exactement ce qu’on demandait pour protéger l’outil industriel, protéger les populations et l’environnement et à terme travailler avec l’Etat sur un projet de reprise », a réagi après l’annonce gouvernementale François Batista, du syndicat CGT des Bouches-du-Rhône. Ce sera désormais à l’Ademe de conduire « la réalisation d’opérations de mise en sécurité », précise le ministère, ajoutant que « le montant de la facture sera évidemment adressé aux liquidateurs ».

title: Patient-reported symptom profiles in vitamin B12 deficiency and pernicious anemia: a cross-sectional study using latent class analysis
content: Pernicious anemia is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by impaired of vitamin B12 absorption and deficiency. Current diagnostic approaches rely on laboratory biomarkers with limitations in sensitivity and specificity, leading to diagnostic uncertainty and potentially delayed and/or suboptimal treatment. The 2024 NICE guidelines acknowledge that treatment frequency should be guided by individual symptom response rather than current one-size-fits-all schedules; however, the symptom heterogeneity underpinning this recommendation remains poorly characterized. We conducted secondary analysis of symptom survey data from 1,117 members of the Pernicious Anaemia Society (PAS) collected between August 2010 and November 2012. We applied latent class analysis (LCA) to 46 self-reported indicators comprising demographic characteristics, symptoms, and comorbid conditions, to identify distinct symptom-based subtypes and assess whether such subgroups can inform more tailored management of PA. Associations between symptom subtypes and diagnostic test results, age when symptoms first started, symptom duration, and treatment satisfaction were examined using chi-square and Fisher’s exact tests. The best model included three distinct symptom subtypes: High Burden (n = 334, 29.9%), Moderate Burden (n = 613, 54.9%), and Low Burden (n = 170, 15.2%). The High Burden subtype exhibited fatigue (99.4%), cognitive dysfunction (97.9% memory loss), neurological manifestations (95.5% clumsiness), and suicidal thoughts (41.6%). Intrinsic factor antibody (IFA) status did not differ significantly across subtypes (χ2 = 1.04, df = 2, p = 0.593). Age at symptom onset differed significantly across subtypes (p = 0.002), with the Low Burden subtype overrepresented in older age groups. The High Burden subtype had the longest diagnostic delays (56.9% >2 years). Standard three-monthly injections showed low satisfaction across all classes (High Burden: 8.5%, Moderate Burden: 23.7%, Low Burden: 30.7%). Symptom-based stratification identifies clinically meaningful subgroups independent of IFA status, supporting tailored, symptom-guided treatment rather than the current piecemeal approach. The inverse association between high symptom burden and age of onset warrants clinical attention. The co-occurrence of markedly elevated rates of depression and suicidal thoughts in the High Burden subtype suggest that integrated mental health assessments should form part of routine clinical management.

title: Talking Past the Machine: Morality, Politeness, and Alignment in Human-AI Dialogue
content: Conversational AI systems produce fluent, socially appropriate responses, yet whether they participate in cooperative communication or merely simulate its surface forms remains unclear - a question central to how these systems are evaluated, trusted, and designed. This study investigates how morality, politeness, and alignment - three dimensions central to cooperative dialogue - function in human-AI interaction compared to human-human conversation. We analyze 15,881 human-ChatGPT and 10,784 human-human multi-turn dialogues, using mixed-effects models to identify which features predict turn-to-turn alignment. We observe a consistent dissociation: AI produces the surface features of cooperative communication without the underlying social architecture. Moral output appears preconfigured rather than negotiated; warmth is generated without face sensitivity; linguistic convergence declines persistently. Most strikingly, the cooperative mechanisms themselves reverse direction: hedging and softening associated with greater accommodation between humans are associated with reduced alignment when produced by AI, and purity framing associated with human divergence coincides with users converging toward the AI. Agency - giving users room to shape the exchange - is the most consistent predictor of alignment across both interaction types, while lower moral assertiveness in more recent models is not accompanied by better cooperation. Together these patterns suggest that AI reproduces the surface of cooperation without the mutual adaptation that grounds it between humans - and, more surprisingly, that mechanisms sustaining human accommodation can run in reverse with AI, suggesting a turn-level view may be insufficient for interaction-level success.

title: Ningaloo Reef corals reveal early fall spawning window for two key species
content:
Curtin University scientists have uncovered an important missing piece in the puzzle of how some coral reefs can recover from climate events, providing information that could help guide future conservation and restoration efforts.
Researchers visited Ningaloo Reef off the Western Australian coast to investigate Porites corals, a group of reef-building corals that play a major role in creating and maintaining reef habitats throughout the Indo-Pacific.
For the first time, the team was able to determine when some of Ningaloo Reef's most important corals reproduce, creating a benchmark that will help scientists track the effects of marine heat waves, assess reef recovery and identify opportunities for restoration. The work is published in the journal Marine Biology.
Survival alone cannot rebuild reefs
Lead author and Ph.D. candidate David Juszkiewicz, from Curtin's Coral Conservation and Research Group, said understanding coral reproduction was essential because reefs could not recover unless corals successfully produced the next generation.
"When people think about reef recovery, they often focus on whether corals survive a bleaching event, but survival is only part of the story," Juszkiewicz said.
"A damaged reef doesn't recover simply because some corals stay alive: it recovers because those corals produce offspring that go on to replenish and rebuild the reef.
"If we don't know when key reef-building corals reproduce, it's much harder to measure whether reefs are recovering successfully, understand the impacts of climate change or support restoration programs that rely on collecting coral eggs and larvae."
Spawning schedules differ among species
The researchers examined 20 coral colonies from Ningaloo Reef and found evidence that two important reef-building species, Porites lutea and Porites lobata, were preparing to spawn during the reef's annual early fall mass spawning period.
The findings provide the first reproductive baseline for these species at Ningaloo.
Researchers found no signs of reproduction in a third species, Porites australiensis, during either sampling period, suggesting it may spawn at a different time of year.
The finding raises the possibility that some of Ningaloo's major reef-building corals do not follow typical reproductive schedules, highlighting the need for year-round monitoring of reproductive activity to better understand how different species respond to heat waves and contribute to reef recovery.
Restoration depends on precise timing
Juszkiewicz said the findings have practical implications for conservation programs that collect coral eggs and larvae for reef restoration projects.
"Timing is everything in coral restoration," Juszkiewicz said.
"If scientists miss a spawning event, they may have to wait another year for the next opportunity.
"Knowing when keystone corals reproduce helps scientists and managers plan restoration programs to ensure they are ready to collect reproductive material at the right time."
Nearby reefs may not replenish Ningaloo
The study also found Ningaloo's Porites corals appear to reproduce in early fall, unlike populations of the same species recorded farther north near Dampier, where spawning has been observed in late spring and early summer.
Senior author associate professor Zoe Richards, leader of the Coral Conservation and Research Group from the School of Molecular and Life Sciences at Curtin University, said these regional differences could influence how reefs recover and replenish themselves after disturbances such as marine heat waves.
"If Ningaloo's corals are reproductively isolated from reefs just 300 km (190 miles) to the north, it means those northern populations may not be able to replenish Ningaloo if its corals are lost during heat waves or cyclones," Richards said.
"They're effectively separate genetic stocks, despite being relatively close geographically."
Heat stress can weaken future reproduction
Dr. Thomas Holmes, program manager for the WA Reef Regen Program at the Western Australian Marine Science Institution, who was not part of this study, said the results were important because heat stress doesn't just affect whether corals live or die.
"It can also reduce reproduction, meaning corals may produce fewer eggs and sperm for years after a major bleaching event," Holmes said.
"That makes reproduction one of the most important indicators of a reef's long-term health and resilience, so this research gives us a benchmark for some of Ningaloo's most important reef-builders.
"If future marine heat waves impact the region, we'll be able to compare reproductive activity and better understand what climate change is doing to the reef's recovery potential. This is incredibly important for informing any future coral regeneration activities."

title: 浙农林大：40年深耕山核桃产业助力乡村共富
content: 金秋九月，浙江临安、淳安以及安徽金寨等重点山核桃主产区迎来一年一度的采收旺季。 山核桃多生长在坡度陡峭的丘陵山地，树高枝脆，以往传统人工攀爬采摘作业风险高，坠落摔伤事故屡有发生。在浙皖山间的山核桃林里，今年却飞来一台名为"云采"的特殊无人机采收装备，通过空中作业助力农户高效采收。 该装备由浙江农林大学研究团队联合浙江理工大学协同研发，依托搭载专属振动采收机构的大疆T40农业无人机，可精准抵近果枝、贴合枝条完成高频振动，促使成熟果梗自然松脱，实现山核桃无损、高效、安全采收。 40余年来，浙江农林大学一代又一代科研团队接续深耕山核桃全产业链，从良种选育、智慧栽培、智能采收，到数字赋能、精深加工、人才培育，全方位突破产业技术壁垒，推动山核桃产业从粗放传统模式向现代化、智能化、高端化转型，让深山小坚果真正成为助力山区群众增收致富的"金果子"。 科研接力，筑牢山核桃产业根基 浙江农林大学坐落于杭州临安，该地素有"中国山核桃之都"的美誉，山核桃产业更是当地赋能乡村振兴、带动群众共同富裕的特色支柱产业。产业发展初期，受种质资源匮乏、栽培技术落后等因素制约，临安山核桃面临良种稀缺、育苗及嫁接成活率低、病虫害频发、大小年差异显著等难题，农户守着山核桃却难以实现稳定增收。 目睹山核桃产业发展困境，当时刚刚毕业留校任教的黄坚钦主动扎根山林，决心攻克产业技术难题，让山核桃真正成为百姓的"致富果"。 此后，黄坚钦深耕山核桃科研助农一线30余年，足迹遍布浙、皖、黔等七省92个县市区。他常年驻守产业基地，深入田间调研取证，摸清山核桃生长习性、病虫害成因及土壤适配规律，同时公开个人技术咨询电话，24小时为全国种植户答疑解惑、提供技术指导。 经过多年反复试验攻坚，团队攻克了山核桃矮化栽培、无性嫁接两大核心技术难题，探明嫁接成活生理生化机制，将山核桃嫁接成活率从28.4%大幅提升至92.7%，挂果周期由传统8年缩短至4年，彻底扭转了山核桃"种植周期长、见效慢"的产业短板，为产业规模化发展筑牢技术根基。 浙农林大专家指导山核桃产业发展 受访者供图 如今，临安山核桃种植面积已扩增至57万亩，产量稳居全国三分之一市场份额。2025年，临安山核桃品牌价值达49.43亿元，连续八年位居全国坚果类品牌榜首。"以前种山核桃全靠天吃饭，跟着黄教授学了科学种植技术后，150多亩林地每年净利润超20万元，实打实变成了致富金果。"山核桃种植大户杨有发的亲身经历，生动印证了科技赋能山核桃产业带来的蜕变红利。 在良种创新迭代、产区技术帮扶领域，浙江农林大学教授王正加团队接续接力、深耕细作。自1997年从教以来，他针对安徽金寨大别山产区山核桃品种老旧、管理粗放、产量偏低、优质资源难以变现等痛点，常年带着研究生深入深山密林开展种质采样、品种筛选、嫁接试验、花期监测等科研工作。 历经多年攻坚突破，团队成功选育出"浙林山1号""皖金1号"等9个国家级优良品种，彻底终结了山核桃产业无审定良种的历史。同时，团队首创湖南山核桃异砧嫁接技术，有效拓宽果树适生区域、增强植株抗逆性，推动产区山核桃亩产从35公斤提升至164公斤，亩产值从1820元跃升至8528元，产业效益实现跨越式提升。 数智赋能，打造产业大脑重塑业态 随着山核桃产业规模化发展持续提速，传统小农分散经营模式的弊端逐步凸显--临安57万亩山核桃林地存在管理标准不统一、新技术推广滞后、林地生态超载、水土流失隐患突出、品牌辨识度低等诸多问题，叠加极端天气频发、市场行情波动等外部影响，传统产业转型升级迫在眉睫。 立足产业核心痛点，浙江农林大学主动扛起校地协同赋能责任，依托林学、计算机、食品科学、环境科学等多学科交叉优势，由该校教授冯海林牵头组建跨学科科研团队，联动临安区农业农村局、林业局等15个职能部门，落地建设全国首个山核桃产业大脑，为传统特色产业装上数字化"智慧引擎"。 为确保数字化平台贴合产业实际、精准解决堵点，冯海林团队深入各主产区、种植合作社、加工企业开展全覆盖调研，精准梳理种植、管护、采收、加工、流通全链条短板，构建起包含环境、品质、生产、市场四大分指数及综合发展指数的"4+1"数字化产业体系，实现产业数据精准画像、科学研判、精准赋能。 在生态管控领域，团队联合黄坚钦团队的科研力量，依托GIS+AHP生态适宜性评价模型，对临安全域57万亩山核桃林地进行精细化分区，精准划定禁种、宜种、限种三类管控区域，科学指导退果还林21517亩，有效缓解林地生态超载、水土流失等问题，实现产业发展与生态保护良性平衡。 在智慧种植赋能上，团队在临安布局11个数字化示范基地，布设127套自动气象站、500余套多维智能传感器，搭建"天空地"一体化智能感知监测网络，实时采集林地气象、土壤水肥、病虫害发生情况、果树长势等核心数据，依托SVM、BP神经网络算法优化产量智能预测模型，彻底打破农户"凭经验种植、靠运气增收"的传统耕作模式。 在品质管控环节，团队制定18项一级指标、3项二级品质指标，运用AI图像分类、质构仪模拟咀嚼等前沿技术，攻克山核桃品质分级、营养量化的行业难题，推动产品品质管控标准化、可视化、精细化，从源头提升产品品质与市场竞争力。 数据互联互通是产业数字化升级的核心抓手。冯海林团队全力攻坚数据融合难题，成功打通临安15个部门的数据孤岛，汇聚整合1500万条山核桃全产业链海量数据，建成一体化数字管理平台，实现种植大户、合作社、加工企业、电商经营主体"一库统管、一网调度"。 ...... 数字化赋能让山核桃产业实现生态、经济、社会效益三重提升。数据显示，2017年至2025年，临安山核桃产业综合指数从92.59攀升至107.33，八年增幅达15.03%，2025年内在品质指数达106.35，产品市场溢价率提升5%。生态效益同步显著改善，林地水土流失量减少15%，森林年新增碳汇15万吨，土壤质量持续优化，农残合格率稳定在99%以上。 全链升级，薪火传承助力共富 从源头良种培育、田间智慧管护，到中端智能采收、绿色加工，再到终端品牌打造、市场增值，浙江农林大学一代又一代科研团队接续攻坚、全链深耕，持续补齐产业短板、深挖产业价值，推动山核桃从传统初级干果零食，向高端健康功能性消费品迭代升级。 针对传统山核桃加工工艺粗放、脱涩成本高、风味营养流失、口感参差不齐等行业痛点，李岩、黄春颖等青年科研团队主动接过科研接力棒，创新研发可食用乳酸菌绿色脱涩工艺，实现低能耗、无污染、原生态加工，最大限度保留山核桃原生风味与营养成分，有效降低加工成本、统一产品品质，大幅提升成品市场口碑。 紧扣大健康产业发展风口，该校专家团队深耕山核桃营养功效科研攻关，成功验证并挖掘出山核桃缓解胰岛素抵抗、调节机体免疫力、降脂降压、辅助减肥等核心健康价值，明晰功能成分合成路径与生物制造机理。依托分子生物学、营养食品化学等前沿技术，题目还研发出核桃功能肽、高品质核桃植物油、营养饮品等高附加值产品，打破了山核桃单一零食的产品格局，推动产业向精细化、功能化、高端化深度转型，有效拉长产业链、提升价值链。 历经一代又一代专家40余年接力攻坚，浙江农林大学科研团队硕果累累：累计收集山核桃优良种质资源585份，制定行业及地方标准6项，授权国家发明专利9件，出版学术专著6部，发表高水平论文200余篇，斩获国家科技进步奖二等奖等6项省部级以上重要奖项。在浙江农林大学科研团队的科技助力下，浙江临安山核桃产量跃升至16300吨，种植面积扩大到57万亩，全区山核桃全产业链产值达50亿元，带动坚果产业实现200亿元产值。在革命老区，团队累计帮扶贵州省锦屏县及革命老区安徽省金寨县贫困户38414户，新增经济效益2.52亿元，以科技之力推动农村产业振兴。 浙江农林大学"金果子"团队负责人表示，今后将持续深耕山核桃全产业链创新攻关，重点突破良种适配优化、智能采收装备迭代、智慧水肥管控等核心技术难题，持续拓宽帮扶版图，以科教赋能特色农业提质增效，让更多深山土特产变身富民兴村的"金果子"，以持久科技力量照亮山区乡村振兴、共同富裕之路。

title: Twenty Years of the Qinghai-Xizang Railway: A Path Toward Harmony Between People and Nature
content:
To build the Qinghai-Xizang Railway, the engineers had to face a series of challenges rarely seen in the history of railway construction worldwide. About a quarter of the railway passes through permafrost regions. In some areas, ice accounts for more than 80 percent of the permafrost, while soil accounts for less than 20 percent. Permafrost is unstable as season changes. It can thaw and sink when temperatures rise in summer, while in winter it will freeze and shrink. So it is easy to crack during construction. Under the combined challenges of high altitude, low temperatures and oxygen deficiency, it was a global engineering challenge for Chinese engineers to ensure the long-term stability of the railway bed.
Faced with such extreme conditions, Chinese engineers and technicians adopted a range of innovative technologies. Along both sides of the railway, tens of thousands of heat-conducting pipes extend deep into the permafrost, draining underground heat to the surface and helping keep the permafrost frozen and stable. The 111-kilometer-long railroad bed with crushed rock ventilation can promote air circulation, carry away heat and reduce subgrade temperatures.
The construction of the Qinghai-Xizang Railway focused not only on engineering safety, but also on ecological conservation throughout the project. A total of 33 wildlife passageways were built along the railway, preserving migration routes for animals on the plateau. The Wudaoliang Bridge alone allows more than 5,000 Tibetan antelopes to pass through each year. Since the railway opened, students in remote mountainous areas have the better access to sound education. Herders can reach markets more easily. Over the past 20 years, the Qinghai-Xizang Railway has transported more than 100 million tons of freight.
The animated video China's New Pulse: How did China build a railway spanning the roof of the world? produced by China Matters, tells the story behind the Qinghai-Xizang Railway. Today, this railway serves as a crucial transport infrastructure for local people with a balanced development between economic growth and ecological conservation.

title: Mi a különbség egy 300 éves és egy mai húslevesrecept között?
content:
Mi a különbség egy 300 éves és egy mai húslevesrecept között?
A húsleves nyilvánvalóan nem magyar étel, van húslevese szinte minden népnek a világon, leveses Kelet-Európán túl Ázsia is, de talán semelyik nép nem válaszol minden ünnepre és krízisre húslevessel úgy, mint mi. Épp ezért a húslevesnek nincs igazán magyar receptje, mindenki más állatból és húsrészekből készíti, még a fűszerezésben és a zöldségekkel való kiegészítésben is lehetnek eltérések. Mindig azt képzeltem, hogy a magyarok ősidők óta kanalazzák a tápláló levet lakodalmon és halotti toron, náthára és másnaposságra, de sok más mellett ez sem mondható régi szokásnak. Legalábbis nem a mai formájában.
A legrégebbi magyar nyomtatott szakácskönyvben rengeteg leves található, de mindben van valami furcsaság. A tehénhús lév nevű recept alatt például azt értik, mikor kenyérrel és tojással keverik el a húslevest. A magyar lév nevű étel már tyúkból készült (nem, Újházy nem csinált még semmit a 17. században), viszont igen egzotikus ízesítéssel: szegfűszeggel, fahéjjal, borssal, gyömbérrel és petrezselyemgyökérrel főzték. A kulcs itt meg is van: ez a zöldség különbözteti meg a magyar húslevest a többitől, máshol petrezselyemgyökeret nem tesznek bele, ez pedig erős, jellegzetes aromát ad a lének. Külföldön élő barátaim gyakran mennek haza pár szál petrezselyemgyökérrel a bőröndjükben, mert úgy érzik, ez az összetevő a magyar húslevesíz kulcsa – és ez már 300 éve így van.
Mivel szinte minden hús főzve készült, a leírásokból nem világos, melyik lé rövidebb, melyik hígabb, melyiket ették magában, melyiket a hússal együtt. A Magyar néprajz szerint is a 18. században terjedt el a húsleves a parasztság körében, minden tájon abból, amihez épp hozzájutottak, de biztosan nem készült gyakran. Fontos húslevesféle volt a kaszás leves, ami füstölt hússal és savanyú ízesítéssel készült.
Ekkor már Európa-szerte hagyománya volt a húsleveskészítésnek, aminek környékbeli divatját nyilván a franciák indították el. François Pierre La Varenne 17. század közepén íródott könyvében már van húsleves, sőt annak luxusverziója, a tojásfehérjés darált hússal tisztított consommé szerepel. Éppen ő volt az, aki megpróbálta lebeszélni olvasóit az egzotikus fűszerek használatáról, ami akkoriban a bőséget és a gazdagságot szimbolizálta, és arra buzdított, hogy használjanak helyi alapanyagokat és fűszereket. Húslevesreceptjéhez épp ezért petrezselymet, metélőhagymát és kakukkfüvet ajánlott. Külön érdekes, hogy míg a magyar konyhában régóta jellemzően egyféle húsból készülnek a levesek – vagy szárnyasból, vagy disznócsontból, vagy marhából –, a francia újkorban úgy keverték a többféle húst, akár az ázsiai konyhákban szokás.
Szakácsmesterségnek könyvecskéje, 1698.: „A tyúkot megtisztogatván egészen tedd fel, forrald fel, párold meg, annakutána spékeld meg, egész szegfűvel szép aprón hasogatott fahajjal, megint tedd fel a fazékba, a maga levét szűrd reá, hasogatott petrezselyemgyökeret melléje, egész borsot, főzd meg jól, mikor megfő, bors, gyömbér; csak úgy egészen tálald fel egynéhány kenyérszeletecskére, a megfőtt petrezselymet szépen felül rakd reá, és vidd az asztalra.”
A húslevesek később, a 18. század során továbbfejlődtek a francia bouillonok és consommék irányában. Simai Kristóf marhalevese a 18. század végén már nagyon hasonlított a mai leveseinkhez, Rézi néni pedig hetven évvel később külön fejezetet szentelt a különféle húsleveseknek, és pár évtizeddel utána ezeknél ugyan kisebb választékban, de közölt húslevesreceptet Zilahy Ágnes és az Első pesti szakácskönyv is.
Nem ugyanaz a helyzet a húslevesnél, mint a gulyásnál, ami tényleg kései találmány, hiszen a húslevesnek fellelhetőek korai változatai már az újkorban is. Olyan fontos szokássá, szimbólummá viszont, amilyen ma, csak később, a 20. században vált. Azóta nem sokat változott, ha nem foglalkozunk azzal a ténnyel, hogy a legtöbben instant leveskockából főzik. Aki rendes húsból készít húslevest, annak már nagy eséllyel valami finom fog a fazékból kikerülni, bár persze ez sem elronthatatlan étel.
A mai éttermi húslevesek a húsfélék mennyiségével és arányával játszanak, a fűszerezésbe pedig gyakran csempésznek egy kis ázsiai vonalat, gyömbért vagy csillagánizst – ebben a tekintetben megyünk visszafelé a gasztrotörténetben.
Napjaink receptjét ezúttal Hetey Mártontól kértük, aki a Nem Ramen nevű pici étteremben főz japán húslevest a Rákóczi téri Vásárcsarnokban. Ott ugyan nem magyar húslevest főz, de mivel sokat foglalkozott a témával, az ő házi húslevesét mutatjuk be.
Hetey Márton húslevese
Alapanyagok egy kb. 10 literes fazékhoz – húsok:
- 1 kilogramm tisztított csirkeláb
- 1,5 kilogramm csirkefarhát/-szárny
- 700 gramm velőscsont
A húsokat hideg vízzel felöntjük úgy, hogy az bőven ellepje őket. Majdnem forrásig melegítjük, közben többször is lehabozzuk, két órán át gyöngyöztetjük. Két óra elteltével hozzáadjuk a zöldségeket és a fűszereket.
Alapanyagok – zöldségek:
- 2 nagy fej vöröshagyma félbevágva, olajon megpirítva
- 1 kis póréhagyma felvágva, olajon megpirítva
- 1 nagy fej fokhagyma félbevágva
- 4 nagyobb fej szárított shiitake gomba
- 10 gramm kombu
- 1 csokor petrezselyemgyökér
- 1 teáskanál fekete bors
- 5 szem borókabogyó
Ezzel egy további órán át gyöngyöztetjük úgy, hogy nem hagyjuk felforrni, majd lekapcsoljuk, és egy órát hűlni hagyjuk. Leszűrjük úgy, hogy a finom törmelék a fazék aljában maradjon. A szűrőben lévő csontokat, zöldségeket ne nyomkodjuk, hagyjuk, hogy maguktól lecsepegjenek. Csak a lére lesz szükség. Amíg a leves fő, el lehet készíteni a betéteket, és félretenni őket, majd a forró alaplé megmelegíti őket a tányérban.
Alapanyagok a levesbetétekhez – zöldségek:
- 500 gramm sárgarépa
- 500 gramm petrezselyemgyökér
- 200 gramm zsenge zöldborsó
- kakukkfű
A répákból batonetteket (hasábokat) vágunk, vajon megpirítjuk őket, sózzuk, egy-két szár kakukkfüvet melléjük dobunk, az egészet felöntjük egy deci alaplével, lefedve megpároljuk, amíg villával átszúrható lesz a répa, de még nem puhul meg egészen. Ha friss a zöldborsó, három percre forró sós vízbe dobjuk és leszűrjük, lehűtjük hideg vízben. Ha nagyon zsenge fagyasztott zöldborsót használunk, egy perc forralás is elég.
Alapanyagok a házi metélthez:
- 300 gramm finomliszt
- 100 gramm búzadara (vagy 400 gramm finomliszt)
- 4 darab közepes méretű tojás
- 4 tojás sárgája
- egy nagy csipet só
Az alapanyagokat addig gyúrjuk, amíg a massza sima lesz és rugalmas, majd lefóliázva hűtőbe tesszük egy-két órára. Ha a leves majdnem kész, tésztagéppel 2 milliméteres vastagságúra nyújtjuk, majd a tésztagép késein áttekerjük, vagy késsel (a tésztát és a deszkát jól belisztezve) metéltre vágjuk. Forró, sós vízben három perc alatt kifőzzük, átszűrjük, majd hideg vízben a csap alatt lemossuk, és beolajozva, lefedve várhatja a tálalást.
Alapanyagok a húsgombóchoz:
- 300 gramm marhanyak, finomra darálva
- 1 tojás
- 2 evőkanál zsemlemorzsa
- 1 kis salotta finomra aprítva
- 1 gerezd fokhagyma reszelve
- petrezselyemzöld
- só, bors
- szerecsendió
A hagymát vajon megpároljuk, utána mehet bele a fokhagyma, a fűszerek és a zsemlemorzsa, valamint a finomra vágott petrezselyem. A hagymát a húsba keverjük a tojással, sóval. Falatnyi gombócokat formázunk, és egy kis sózott alaplében vagy sós vízben, halkan gyöngyöztetve 10-15 perc alatt megfőzzük őket.
A kész, leszűrt levesről lekanalazzuk a zsírt, és félretesszük. Tálalás előtt a levest sózzuk: a legtöbb embernek egy deci levesenként egy gramm só az ideális arány.
Tálaláskor mindenből halmozunk a tányérba, majd lassan felöntjük a levessel. Egy evőkanál zsírt teszünk a tetejére.
Sorozatunkban fontos magyar ételek legrégebbi és egyik legújabb receptjét mutatjuk be egymás mellett. A sorozat első részében a gulyáslevesről volt szó, a másodikban a hortobágyi húsos palacsintáról, a harmadikban a töltött paprikáról.

title: Bečki stručnjaci predstavili mogućnosti ekološke obnove Miljacke
content:
Bečki stručnjaci predstavili mogućnosti ekološke obnove Miljacke
Na radionici pod nazivom "Od regulisanog do prirodnijeg vodotoka - iskustva Beča za Miljacku" analizirani su modeli transformacije gradskih vodotoka i otvorena mogućnost zajedničkog učešća dva grada u budućim projektima Evropske unije, saopćili su iz Međunarodnog ureda Grada Beča u Sarajevu.
U okviru šireg projekta "Čista rijeka Miljacka", Grad Sarajevo za 2026. godinu planira realizaciju 47 projekata koji obuhvataju obnovu kanalizacione infrastrukture, bolje upravljanje otpadom i mjere zaštite od poplava.
Predstavnica Grada Sarajeva i koordinatorica radne grupe Senada Dizdar istakla je da samo korito Miljacke ne predstavlja glavni rizik od izlijevanja, već da najveći problem čine manje ucijevljene pritoke čiji kapaciteti ne mogu prihvatiti velike količine vode tokom obilnih padavina.
Austrijski stručnjaci iz službi Wiener Gewässer (MA 45) i Wien Kanal predstavili su bečka iskustva na primjeru rijeke Liesingbach, koja je iz strogo regulisanog kanala uspješno transformisana u prirodniji vodotok.
Bečki tim, koji su činili Thomas Ofenböck, Karin Weichselberger, Isabella Schild i Thilo Lehmann, naglasio je da se modernim pristupima moraju istovremeno rješavati i problem suša i visokih temperatura usljed klimatskih promjena, a ne samo zaštita od poplava.
Predstavnici Grada Sarajeva pokazali su poseban interes za bečke metode razdvajanja otpadnih i oborinskih voda, dok su goste iz Beča zanimali lokalni planovi zaštite te izazovi koordinacije između različitih nivoa vlasti u Bosni i Hercegovini.
Predstavnici Instituta za vodoprivredu najavili su da će u narednom planskom ciklusu detaljno definisati konkretne mjere za pojedinačna vodna tijela Miljacke i njenih pritoka.
Učesnici su se dotakli i pitanja uključivanja građana u procese planiranja. Dok je Beč predstavio svoje sistemske modele participacije, sarajevska strana je podijelila iskustva iz javnih rasprava i inovativnih pilot-projekata, ukazavši na problem spore integracije građanskih prijedloga u zvanične dokumente zbog podijeljenih nadležnosti.
Zaključeno je da bi se renaturacijom pojedinih dionica Miljacke značajno poboljšao kvalitet vode u gradu, ali i da se austrijska rješenja ne mogu direktno prepisati, već se moraju pažljivo prilagoditi specifičnim lokalnim uslovima Sarajeva, saopćili su iz Međunarodnog ureda Grada Beča u Sarajevu.

title: Memories of childhood scents associated with joy are encoded by neurons generated shortly after birth
content:
A study published in PLOS Biology by Jules Dejou and colleagues shows that neurons developing around the time of birth in the olfactory bulb granule-cell layer (a region of the brain) are the ones encoding the memories of scents associated with joy in childhood. A separate primer by Chloé Guillaume and Elisa Galliano published in PLOS Biology discusses these results. In the study, juvenile mice exposed to attractive odors while in an enriched playful environment showed a preference for that odor in adulthood more than mice exposed to the same odor while in normal housing.
Memories evoked by odors are often unusually vivid and emotionally powerful. This is particularly the case when they originate in childhood. Compared with memories triggered by visual or auditory cues, autobiographical memories triggered by odors tend to come from earlier periods of life and are more often associated with positive emotions. Repeated exposure to the same odor in a consistent emotional context can gradually create strong associations that persist for many years. Such memories may be linked not to a specific reward, but to a broader sense of comfort, happiness, or well-being associated with familiar childhood experiences.
Olfaction is especially important early in life because it is functional from birth and can guide essential behaviors before other sensory systems are fully developed. The olfactory system also has unusually direct connections with brain regions involved in memory, reward, and emotion, including the amygdala, hippocampus, orbitofrontal cortex, and related limbic structures (a network of brain regions that control emotion and memory).
Odor information is initially processed in the olfactory bulb, where granule cells (a type of small neuron) and other interneurons (neurons that transmit signals between other neurons) help refine sensory signals before they are transmitted to higher brain regions. Many of these olfactory interneurons are generated early in life and can be shaped by early sensory experience, making them plausible substrates for long-lasting odor memories.
To identify the neurons responsible for encoding olfactory memories from childhood and to understand the neural mechanism that allows them to play an important role in forming a person’s identity, the study authors started with a survey involving 647 human participants. Participants were asked to recall an odorant that was significant in their childhood, going back as far as possible in time. They were then asked to rate the pleasantness and the presence of six basic emotions (happiness, surprise, fear, disgust, sadness, and anger) associated with that smell.
Results of this survey showed that the ratings were highest for positive emotions, namely happiness and pleasantness, followed by surprise. Ratings of negative emotions were lower. Participants were also asked how many times the event that led to their earlier odor memories occurred. Seventy-three percent of participants reported that the event occurred more than five times.
Finally, participants rated the hedonic value (the degree to which something is considered pleasant or unpleasant) of their childhood odorant, which they found to be predominantly pleasant. The authors used another dataset to see whether those smells are intrinsically pleasant or whether participants only perceived them that way. The results indicated that those smells do tend to be intrinsically pleasant, indicating that individuals prefer to make pleasant odors a part of their autobiographical memory.
Based on the human survey results, the researchers developed a mouse model. They divided 23-day-old (juvenile) mice into two groups. One group was exposed up to their 33rd day of life to an attractive odor such as limonene, citronellol, or camphor while the mice were in a positive, enriched, playful environment.
This pairing between the odor and the environment was repeated five times during the 10 days of the experiment. It was done every other day for 2 hours. The second, control group of mice was also exposed to the same odor, but in their ordinary housing. The study authors assessed the emotions of the mice by registering their ultrasonic vocalizations, with more numerous and higher frequency vocalizations indicating a more positive emotional state.
Later, when the mice were 2 months old (i.e., young adults), the study authors tested whether they showed a preference for that odor. The mice that learned to associate the odor with an enriched environment and positive emotions indeed showed a greater preference for it compared to mice that experienced it in their ordinary housing. The researchers observed that this memory recall relied on increased functional connectivity in the brain’s reward system.
Investigation of the neural basis of this smell memory found that neurons born around the first day of life in the olfactory bulb granule-cell layer tended to be particularly activated by the odor the mice learned to associate with positive emotions as juveniles. When these neurons were silenced using optogenetics (a biological technique that uses light to control neurons that have been genetically modified to express light-sensitive ion channels), the preference for the odor was reduced, suggesting that these neurons are a key part of the early memory recall mechanism.
However, by 6 months of age, that memory was gone, unless the mice were periodically re-exposed to the scent. In these older mice, memory persistence was no longer dependent on the neonatal-born granule cells. Instead, the persistence of the memory was associated with a large-scale reorganization of the brain’s functional networks, shifting away from the reward system to rely on strengthened connections within the olfactory-limbic system.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of childhood odor memories and their role in overall psychological functioning. However, it should be noted that while the initial survey was conducted on humans, the experimental manipulations were conducted on mice. While mice and humans share many physiological similarities, they are still very different species, and the exact neural network mechanisms in humans might differ.
The primer, “Neurons generated shortly after birth encode the scent of early-life happiness,” was authored by Chloé Guillaume and Elisa Galliano. The paper, “Positive early-life olfactory memory is rooted in the olfactory bulb and triggers large-scale changes beyond the olfactory system,” was authored by Jules Dejou, Anna Athanassi, Théo Brunel, Marc Thevenet, Anne Didier, and Nathalie Mandairon.

title: A Cutting-Edge English Initiative Replaces Lawnmowers With Scythes to Restore Wildflowers and Save the Bees
content:
A Cutting-Edge English Initiative Replaces Lawnmowers With Scythes to Restore Wildflowers and Save the Bees
English Heritage has recruited volunteers to mow meadows the old-fashioned way at some of its historic sites
Scything has come quaintly back to the English countryside. The conservation charity English Heritage recently recruited volunteers willing to cut grass in the way of their ancestors—with the Grim Reaper’s blade. They’re now scything through Somerset meadows in exchange for bread and cheese.
The three-year project aims to maintain English meadows without overly disturbing their natural inhabitants—specifically, the endangered shrill carder bumblebee.
“If you take mowers in here, there’s a risk that you can hurt them,” English Heritage site manager Ed McGregor tells BBC Radio Somerset.
According to the Bumblebee Conservation Trust, which is collaborating with English Heritage on the project, the shrill carder bumblebee (Bombus sylvarum) is among the United Kingdom’s rarest and most vulnerable bee species. It lives in only five areas, one of which is the southwestern county of Somerset.
The volunteer scythers, trained by Somerset’s Exmoor National Park Authority, have begun working in the meadow of the historic Muchelney Abbey. Soon, they’ll be scything grass at English Heritage-managed sites across the county, per a statement from the charity.
“Scything is a wonderful example of how traditional skills can still have a role in addressing modern challenges,” says volunteer and community engagement manager Ginny Slade in the statement. “We hope to help create the diverse, flower-rich habitats that pollinators need while also preserving knowledge and skills that have shaped our landscapes.”
The scythe is one of agriculture’s pivotal tools. Its exact—likely ancient—origins remain mysterious, but historians know the scythe became common in Europe around the eighth century. Composed of a thin, very sharp blade attached to a curved wooden handle, the tool is swung from left to right by a standing scyther. According to the Museum of English Rural Life, an experienced reaper could cut down two acres of wheat in a day.
“You need a level of physical fitness, but it’s also about enthusiasm and the passion to learn heritage skills,” Slade tells the Guardian’s Steven Morris. “It’s a repetitive movement. You find your rhythm and zone into it. You can really connect with the meadow, the landscape.”
The shrill carder bumblebee’s population has shrunk significantly with the decline of England’s flower-rich grasslands, per the statement. Taking a lawnmower to existing meadows, like those around Muchelney Abbey, can actually help wildflowers grow, and in turn provide bees with pollen. But the invasive machine can kill the bees, which nest in the ground. As Joseph O’Shea, a project officer at the Bumblebee Conservation Trust, tells the London Times’ Will Pavia, electric mowers are “so fast that things can’t get away.”
The volunteer scythers won’t just be landscaping in a bee-friendly fashion. They’ll also be performing wildlife surveys. Per the statement, the volunteers will record the number of bees, which flowers are in bloom, which plants the bees are visiting and how far the insects travel from their nests.
Scythes haven’t been a common farmer’s tool for centuries. They first became popular as a more efficient alternative to ancient handheld sickles—hooked blades that required reapers to work at crop level. But in time, scythes were replaced by horse-drawn mowers, then mechanized combines. As riding lawnmowers and combines cut grass and wheat across England, the volunteer scythers are enjoying a quiet, pastoral reversion.
“It’s incredibly satisfying, and hearing the swish through the ground is amazing,” McGregor tells BBC Radio Somerset. “It’s great exercise, and [it’s] been fun learning about its heritage.”

title: Rare snails lay eggs during car journey to zoo
content:
Rare snails lay eggs during car journey to zoo
- Published
A rare snail found in just one lake in the UK started laying eggs on its six-hour journey from Wales to Kent, as a zoo joined a nationwide effort to save the species.
Glutinous snails are no bigger than a fingertip and used to be widespread across UK water ways.
It is thought habitat disruption and environmental changes reduced their population to such an extent that they are only now found in Llyn Tegid, a lake in Eryri National Park, also known as Snowdonia.
Wingham Wildlife Park near Canterbury has taken some of the wild population to breed and release into the wild. Samantha Eden, assistant curator, said the zoo started with six snails and recently started a new colony.
Despite their slow reputation, the breeding efforts are off to a flying start, Eden said.
"I brought 24 snails back from Wales at the start of July," she said.
"It was a six hour drive, and by the time I'd arrived back at the park I had about 12 egg pods in the carry containers that we were using. They'd laid eggs literally whilst we were driving.
"We started, with one of the ponds, with just six adult snails. We recently moved 130 babies out of that pond to start a new colony."
Hannah Ellins, head of reptiles and invertebrates, said: "We do a lot of work with exotics, but it's cool being able to help our animals here."
She added: "We'll keep breeding them and then hopefully we'll eventually then release them into the wild and help wild populations."
The scheme is part of a wider national effort to protect the very rare species.
Wingham Wildlife Park is joining Askham Bryan Wildlife Park in York and Longleat in Wiltshire, along with Dudley and Chester zoos, with the Freshwater Habitats Trust searching for suitable water bodies where the snails could eventually be released.

title: Genomic Research as a Critical Pathway to Diagnosis for Individuals with Rare Disease
content: Many individuals with rare monogenic disease remain molecularly undiagnosed due to challenges accessing genetic testing, ambiguity in interpretation of uncertain variants, and latency between novel disease-gene discovery and adoption into clinical pipelines. The Rare Genomes Project (RGP) provides a remote, research-based genomic sequencing (GS) service for rare disease families to overcome diagnostic barriers while advancing the understanding of the genetic basis of rare disease. Short-read GS and family-centered analysis were performed to identify causes of primary disease. Variants meeting return criteria were clinically confirmed and returned to families. Since 2017, RGP enrolled clinically heterogeneous, undiagnosed rare disease families from all fifty states, Washington DC, and Puerto Rico. Findings were returned to 272 of 1014 sequenced families, resulting in a solve rate of 23.3% and a returned strong candidate rate of 3.5%. Condition-specific return rates ranged from 15% to 40% with many families receiving a result in a known disease gene after healthcare access challenges. Research interventions contributed to returns in 16% of all families and included variants in recently discovered or non-coding disease genes, additional functional studies to resolve variant uncertainty, and real-time data sharing to empower novel disease-gene discovery. RGP demonstrates that a research-based, patient-driven remote sequencing study can effectively bridge a diagnostic gap for rare disease families underserved in current clinical care. This study also underscores the clinical utility of GS with frequent re-analysis and highlights the critical continued role of research in variant interpretation, method innovation, and genomic knowledge base expansion for rare disease diagnosis.

title: How freediving helps Indonesia’s Bajau preserve traditions and conserve marine life
content:
- The Bajau people of Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines have traditionally harvested the sea through freediving.
- A recent ban on compressor-assisted diving in Indonesia’s West Nusa Tenggara province has made traditional freediving skills more valuable than ever.
- On Sumbawa, one of the province’s largest islands, traditional fishers and a local NGO are working together to preserve Bajau diving techniques and to manage local marine and fisheries resources in harmony with traditional management practices.
POTO TANO, Indonesia — Mahari sits at the front of the boat, cigarette in hand, surveying the conditions of the waters off Poto Tano, a small fishing community on the island of Sumbawa, Indonesia. As ketua, the leader of this group of Bajau octopus fishers, Mahari decides which tool they will use today. He silently surveys the waters while the rest of the group sits back and waits for his cue.
The Bajau people are an Indigenous ethnic group spanning Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines. Traditionally living mostly on boats, Bajau people have harvested from the sea through traditional freediving for generations. In Sumbawa, a recent ban on dives assisted by an air compressor, a dangerous diving technique that provides the diver with continuous air, means these traditional methods have become more valuable than ever. With the right skills, freediving can be gentler on both the environment and the body than more destructive modern practices.
Through expeditions like this one, Mahari and the other fishermen in his community work in cooperation with local NGOs to ensure this knowledge is passed to new generations.
‘Pocong time’
Depending on current and water visibility, Bajau fishers typically use one of two methods to catch octopus. If there is low visibility or a strong current, they will use a “shell” tool adorned with hooks, which they let go in the water and trail behind their boat. If there is better visibility and a weaker current, they enter the water to freedive and use the pocong.
The pocong, the Indonesian word for “ghost,” is a fishing tool resembling a fake octopus made from wood and felt. Using the pocong, the Bajau dive to around 15–20 meters (50-65 feet) and dangle this decoy alongside the reef to lure an octopus. When their prey responds curiously to this lure, the fishers either spear the live octopus or grab it by hand. While it may sound simple, this is actually a very skilled technique, as they cannot let the octopus touch the pocong. “They will immediately realize it’s fake and swim away,” says one of the fishermen tells Mongabay. “Only 10 people in their community can use the pocong. You need strength and skill.”
On the boat, Mahari suddenly makes his pronouncement, “It’s Pocong time.”
The incredible skills and abilities of the Bajau freedivers are widely known and documented, earning them a global reputation as sea nomads and sparking studies in human physiology and genetics.
Mahari recalls some of his earliest memories in the ocean with a gleam in his eye, “As a Bajau, we know how to dive for as long as we can remember.” Another fisher, Nadir, tells Mongabay: “Bajau people can tell directions without GPS, but by reading the stars, the wind, the air, and the currents. One week after children are born, we bring them to the sea.”
In recent years, many Bajau fishers have felt the pull towards compressor diving as a more economically viable method of harvesting marine species. Often acting as the sole providers for their families, many feel pressure to bring home enough fish to support their households.
Compressor diving is a controversial and dangerous practice where divers breathe in surface air pumped by a compressor through a long hose, allowing them to stay underwater much longer and deeper than they would if freediving. Extending their time underwater both increases their chances of finding valuable species and of returning home with a larger catch. “With compressor diving, you can stay underwater for much longer,” one of the fishers, Well, tells Mongabay. “If you get more octopus, you get more money. There’s a temptation. We’re human, right?”
But compressor diving systems are often improvised, with no safety checks. The risks and impacts of this form of diving include decompression sickness, air embolisms, paralysis and chronic disabilities, long-term mobility issues and heightened drowning risks. While freediving does have some known health risks, including injuries from pressure changes, they pale in comparison to the risks associated with diving with compressors.
Acknowledging these risks, the Jari Foundation has started to work in partnership with many Bajau fishermen to ease their transition away from compressor diving and towards traditional freediving practices.
Jari is a marine-based program focused on management, ecotourism and community development that currently works across the islands of Lombok and Sumbawa. Together with the local government and a small group of Bajau fishermen, Jari has established a community-based fishery group called PELITA [Persaudaraan Nelayan Gurita (Octopus Fishermen Brotherhood)], says Hani Nusantari, who runs Jari alongside her husband, Boen. PELITA currently consists of around 40 octopus fishermen, many of whom previously relied on compressor diving. “Recognizing the long-term impacts this practice was having on their health, they chose to return to traditional freediving methods while also becoming actively involved in marine conservation initiatives and ecotourism,” Hani says.
Literally translating to “light”, PELITA is named after the traditional oil lamp that once illuminated the homes of fishing families. “PELITA represents a guiding light for coastal communities, bringing people together to care for the sea, strengthen solidarity among fishers, and ensure that marine resources continue to support future generations,” Hani says.
Through PELITA, Hani says she hopes to strengthen fishers’ livelihoods by supporting a return to traditional practices and by combining traditional knowledge with conservation, fisheries management and alternative livelihood projects. This type of fisheries management is supported by more than just the male fishers of PELITA. Hani initiated Women for Marine Conservation (WMC) in 2022 to strengthen community participation in conservation and fisheries management. Today, WMC members are also involved in fisheries data collection, tourism activities, environmental education and community organization.
The compressor ban
Indonesia’s fishery laws do not explicitly mention compressors, but regulations that ban destructive and unsafe fishing gear and methods indirectly prohibit them. In 2020, the West Nusa Tenggara provincial government added a regulation that specifically stipulates a ban on compressor diving. However, Jari’s Boen notes that the problem has not disappeared entirely: “The problem is that [some people] keep doing compressor diving at night when there is no surveillance. One night, we took our fishermen group out at night, and we found 50–60 compressor divers just in this area.”
All the PELITA fishermen have now stopped compressor diving. One of them, Wandra, says that many of his friends got sick, became paralyzed, or even died because of compressor dives gone wrong. Fellow fisherman Well decided to stop after becoming paralyzed for a month at a time, on three separate occasions. Mahari says he has been paralyzed 30 times, “I would go to the chamber, get healthy, and then go to the compressor to get back.”
Compressor diving also has long-term physical impacts on freedivers’ abilities. “When they breathe with the compressor for a long time, it’s a challenge to return to freediving because they’re used to the compressor,” Hani says.
Despite the known risks, implementing the compressor diving ban has been complex, Boen says: “Some people were happy with the regulation, but for the Bajau people there were mixed emotions. Many families faced uncertainty because they depended heavily on marine resources for their livelihoods, so we had a stakeholder meeting.” In December 2025, Jari proposed the addition of an article to place the Poto Tano village government in charge of governing its own marine resources, he says. “The problem is the Bajau are in the sea every day,” adds Mahari. “We suggest ecological management, so limits on catch and size. Everything is enough for everybody. The problem is when there are greedy people who take more than what they need.”
The fishers agree with conservation, Hani says, “It’s more a discussion about management approaches, where we propose sustainable use and local stewardship rather than unrestricted fishing.”
Rights-based fishery management
Boen and Mahari support the idea of traditional fisheries leading their own management under a rights-based fisheries management model practiced in other countries such as Canada and Australia. “Our ideal situation is community-based fisheries led by communities and traditional ecological knowledge,” Boen says.
Traditional practices already support conservation, Wandra says, “We close two to three areas at a time for a few months to help the fishing grounds regenerate.” If the fishers catch an octopus that is too small, they will release it, Well adds. Compared with industrial fisheries, the tools, boats and catches of the Bajau people are also limited to ensure sustainable practices.
The article on village self-governance of marine resources was just recently approved, and JARI and PELITA are working to develop further village-level mechanisms and local regulations.
What does the future hold for the Bajau?
It is too early to say whether the community can sustain a shift away from compressor diving. In the meantime, Hani is passionate about ensuring traditional Bajau practices are not lost. “The reality is that the majority of Poto Tano don’t know about their traditional culture,” Hani says. “The Bajau people have always had a strong storytelling culture, so we want to figure out how to pass down this knowledge in a way that makes sense to them.” There are nascent plans to create a Bajau museum in Poto Tano, she adds.
Kadir, another of the small number of fishermen skilled in using the pocong, says that “the younger generation has seen how others have been impacted by the compressor, so they don’t want to pursue it anymore.” Some youth, including Kadir’s son, are now involved in conservation, marine ecotourism and ecological monitoring.
“Bajau people will always rely on the sea,” Mahari says. “Now that I have a family and children, I think a lot more about how our kids are going to be impacted. There’s an interest in traditional technologies, but now there is also interest in gathering more data so that we can protect the reef better. Understanding trends over larger spatial areas would help us strengthen our management. My niece is now studying marine science.”

title: Less than 4 years from development goals deadline, progress shows what’s possible
content:
Less than 4 years from development goals deadline, progress shows what’s possible
For Benin, making progress on the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) has meant finding new ways to finance development.
The West African country has increased domestic revenue by 0.5 per cent of GDP each year for the past decade, issued Africa’s first SDG bond in 2021 and used the resulting funding to expand access to education and drinking water, Aristide Medenou, Benin’s minister of economic cooperation, said on Friday.
Access to drinking water there has increased from 40 per cent to 80 per cent in the past five years, Mr. Medenou said, while a new industrial zone launched in 2021 has created 25,000 jobs.
“If a country is not able to increase the domestic revenue, the country cannot go forward in implementing the SDGs,” Mr. Medenou said at the UN’s annual SDG Moment event ahead of the General Assembly’s High-Level Week in New York.
Even as the world remains far from achieving the SDGs, Mr. Medenou said Benin offers a concrete example of governments translating commitments into beneficial policies.
Many goals off track
In 2015, all UN Member States adopted the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, committing to 17 SDGs focusing on issues such as ending poverty, protecting the planet and ensuring lasting peace.
Member States set a target to achieve these goals by 2030. However, the UN’s most recent progress report indicated that progress on the goals is slow and uneven – of the 139 targets with available trend data, 36 per cent are on track or making moderate progress.
“Progress was never automatic,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres said on Friday. “It was earned through the determination of people, communities and countries.”
SDGs create meaningful progress
At UN Headquarters in New York, UN officials and world leaders highlighted both the gains made over the past decade – and the scale of the remaining challenge.
Nearly a billion people have gained access to safely managed drinking water since the SDGs were adopted, and 1.2 billion have gained access to safely managed sanitation. Electricity now reaches 92 per cent of the world’s population – up from 87 per cent in 2015 – and internet access has risen from 40 per cent to 74 per cent.
But 49 per cent of SDG targets with available trend data are progressing too slowly, while 15 per cent have fallen below their 2015 baselines, according to the SDG Progress Report.
Food insecurity affected 2.1 billion people in 2025, while one in 10 people still live in extreme poverty, said General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman.
The world faces a $4 trillion annual SDG financing gap, while official development assistance fell by a record 23 per cent in 2025. In many countries, debt payments outstrip spending on social services.
The world is currently on track to warm by around 2.8 degrees Celsius this century, well above the 1.5-degree threshold set by the Paris Agreement.
“These are losses that many cannot absorb,” Mr. Rahman said. “For many of us, sustainability is a matter of life and death.”
Young leaders call for action
Suzuka Nakamura of Japan and Adelin Pierre of Haiti, two of the UN’s Young Leaders for the SDGs, called on governments to act with the same urgency that led them to agree on the SDGs 11 years ago.
“To the leaders in this room and around the world, you made this promise,” Ms. Nakamura said. “We are asking you to keep it.”
Mr. Medenou also stressed the need to involve the private sector, saying governments “cannot do it alone.”
‘Powerful headwinds’ to SDG progress
Mr. Guterres said the lives that have been improved by SDG implementation demonstrate that multilateral cooperation can produce tangible improvements when governments act.
He explained that the pursuit of the goals has helped reduce child and maternal mortality, prevent millions of new HIV infections, and expand access to education, social protection, renewable energy and other services.
But progress faces “powerful headwinds” such as conflicts, weakened international cooperation, the climate crisis, attacks on the rights of women and girls, and debt and investment constraints, Mr. Guterres said.
“The promises governments made in adopting the Goals are not being kept,” he said. “It is time to keep them.”
Peace a prerequisite
The Secretary-General emphasised the priorities of fighting inequality, protecting the planet, financing sustainable development and using all available tools and technologies to accelerate progress.
He called for greater investment in education and health, a just transition to renewable energy, stronger financing and debt support for developing countries, and greater use of technology such as “responsible” artificial intelligence.
Mr. Guterres said peace is both a foundation and an enabler of sustainable development, stressing that the world needs renewed efforts to secure peace everywhere.
There’s still time
With four years until the deadline, speakers emphasised the need to convert commitments into results while reaching the people who remain the furthest behind.
UN Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) President Amar Bendjama said progress is possible when ambition is matched with implementation.
For the young leaders at the event, the impending deadline is not a reason to abandon the goals, but a reason to act with increased urgency.
“There is still time to act, but we need to move together,” Ms. Nakamura said. “We are not giving up hope on the SDGs, and neither should you.”

title: New MRI measure reveals how closely blood flow matches brain cells' energy needs
content:
Researchers from the Mark and Mary Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute (Stevens INI) at the Keck School of Medicine of USC have developed a new, noninvasive way to examine how blood flow and cellular organization align across the layers of the living human brain.
The study, published in Nature Communications, introduces the cerebral blood flow–cell-body staining intensity similarity index, or CCSI. It may help scientists understand how blood vessels, cells and energy-producing machinery work together to support brain function.
The cerebral cortex, the brain's folded outer layer, contains layers with different numbers and types of cells. These cells need a continuous supply of oxygen and nutrients, but researchers have had limited tools for studying how blood flow matches their distribution in the living brain.
"The brain has almost no ability to store energy, so its cells depend on a constant and carefully regulated supply from the bloodstream," said Fanhua Guo, co-first author of the study and a researcher at the Stevens INI. "Our new measure gives us a way to study how well that energy supply is positioned to meet cellular demands in different parts of the cortex."
Mapping blood flow across cortical layers
The researchers used arterial spin labeling, or ASL, a noninvasive MRI technique that magnetically labels water in the blood and tracks it into brain tissue. A powerful 7 Tesla MRI scanner measured blood flow throughout the brain at a resolution of one cubic millimeter.
The study included 30 healthy adults; 14 returned for a second scan to test the consistency of the measurements.
The team divided the cortex into 360 regions and examined blood flow at multiple depths. They compared those patterns with cell-body staining data from BigBrain, a detailed three-dimensional digital reconstruction of a human brain that maps how densely cells are packed throughout the cortex.
"Conventional brain imaging often averages information across the full thickness of the cortex, but the cortex is not a uniform sheet," said Chenyang Zhao, co-first author of the study and a researcher at the Stevens INI.
"By imaging blood flow at very high resolution, we can begin to see how perfusion changes from the outer surface of the cortex to its deeper layers."
"Neuroscience is entering an era where we can combine advanced brain imaging with detailed maps of the brain's cells, gene expression and metabolism," said Ravi R. Bhatt, Ph.D., a postdoctoral scholar at the Stevens INI. "Each map provides a different view of the brain, and together they reveal patterns that would otherwise remain hidden."
The resulting CCSI score measured how closely blood flow and cellular density followed the same pattern across cortical depth. Higher scores indicated that cell-dense layers tended to receive more blood flow.
Blood flow and cellular organization aligned in most cortical regions, meaning that within a given region, blood flow tended to be highest in the layers with the most cells, although the strength varied across the brain. Alignment was strongest in primary visual and sensorimotor areas, which support vision, movement and touch.
Connecting blood flow to the brain's energy system
To clarify what CCSI represents biologically, the researchers compared it with maps of mitochondrial activity, cell types and gene expression.
Mitochondria convert nutrients and oxygen into usable energy. Regions where blood flow and cellular organization aligned more strongly also had greater mitochondrial respiratory capacity, the maximum rate at which mitochondria can produce energy, suggesting the regions may be better equipped to meet local energy demands.
The relationship involved mitochondrial capacity, not simply the number of mitochondria. Total blood flow did not show the same association, suggesting CCSI reveals metabolic organization that standard blood-flow measurements may miss.
"Blood flow tells us how much blood reaches a region, but it does not tell us how that supply is distributed in relation to the cells that need it," said Danny JJ Wang, Ph.D., senior and corresponding author of the study, professor of neurology and director of imaging technology innovation at the Stevens INI.
"CCSI adds that missing spatial information and may provide a more biologically meaningful picture of how vascular supply supports energy use across cortical layers."
CCSI was also associated with capillary endothelial cells, which line the smallest blood vessels and help regulate how blood reaches surrounding tissue.
It was also associated with mature oligodendrocytes, brain cells that produce the protective myelin coating around nerve fibers. Because oligodendrocytes also support nerve fibers' metabolism, the finding suggests they may help connect vascular supply with neurons' energy needs.
Gene activity further linked CCSI to energy metabolism, blood vessel development, vascular organization and healthy mitochondria. Together, the findings suggest that the alignment of blood flow and cellular structure reflects a coordinated system involving blood vessels, supporting cells and energy production.
Helping explain the brain's most complex regions
The researchers also asked whether CCSI could help explain the relationship between brain structure and function. That connection is usually close in sensory and motor regions but less direct in higher-order association regions, which support memory, reasoning and attention.
The researchers tested this using structural-functional coupling analysis that predicts brain function from the cortex's structural features. Adding CCSI significantly improved the models' ability to predict function in these higher-order regions. The findings suggest that metabolic and vascular factors shape brain function in ways cellular structure alone cannot explain.
"This study bridges several levels of brain organization, from blood vessels and mitochondria to cells, cortical layers and gene expression," said Arthur W. Toga, Ph.D., director of the Stevens INI.
"By bringing these sources of information together, the researchers have created a new framework for investigating how the living brain supports its extraordinary energy demands."
The study does not establish that stronger alignment causes more efficient energy use. Its molecular and cellular comparisons relied on reference atlases from a limited number of postmortem donors, and CCSI currently measures groups rather than individuals. Future studies will test larger, more varied populations and explore changes linked to aging and neurological or psychiatric conditions.
Disruptions in blood flow, metabolism and oligodendrocyte function occur in Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis, schizophrenia and epilepsy. CCSI could eventually help researchers study how these systems become disconnected.
"Understanding the healthy relationship between vascular supply and cellular organization is an important first step," said Neda Jahanshad, Ph.D., professor of neurology and biomedical engineering at the Stevens INI.
"The long-term goal is to determine whether changes in this relationship can reveal early signs of disease or help us evaluate treatments aimed at restoring brain metabolism and vascular health. The hope is that CCSI may eventually offer insight into early signs of disease and potential treatments."
