title: Ethiopia’s Wheat Revolution Delivers a Powerful Message: Africa Can Feed Itself — President Taye
content:
Ethiopia’s Wheat Revolution Delivers a Powerful Message: Africa Can Feed Itself — President Taye
Addis Ababa, September 24, 2026 (FMC) — Ethiopia’s transformation from a wheat-importing country into one of Africa’s largest wheat producers is demonstrating the continent’s capacity to strengthen its own food security, President Taye Atske-Selassie told the 81st United Nations General Assembly.
Addressing the General Assembly in New York, President Taye highlighted Ethiopia’s rapid progress in wheat production, supported by the introduction and expansion of climate-resilient wheat varieties.
He presented the transformation against a backdrop of growing pressure on global food systems, where access to food has increasingly become a strategic concern and disruptions to supply chains can have consequences far beyond national borders.
“At a time where food provision has become a political battleground and the global food supply hangs precariously in the balance, we send a clear message that Africa can feed itself,” President Taye said.
Ethiopia’s experience, he noted, demonstrates the potential for African countries to harness their agricultural resources, expand domestic production and strengthen resilience against external food-supply pressures.
The transformation from importer to major producer also reflects Ethiopia’s broader emphasis on building productive capacity as a foundation for sustainable development. By expanding climate-resilient agricultural production, the country is seeking to strengthen food availability while contributing to wider economic resilience.
President Taye’s remarks place Ethiopia’s wheat gains within a broader continental context: Africa’s large agricultural potential can be translated into greater food production when supported by appropriate technologies, investment and climate-resilient approaches.
The President linked food security with Ethiopia’s wider development priorities, including renewable energy, connectivity, manufacturing and urban development, while calling for genuine and sustained regional and international cooperation to sustain and scale up these gains.
Ethiopia’s wheat transformation, therefore, was presented at the UNGA not simply as a national agricultural achievement, but as evidence of the capacity for African countries to build stronger, more resilient food systems and advance toward greater food self-reliance.

title: Europe's crackdown halves shadow fleet ships sailing under false flags, report says
content:
Europe's crackdown halves shadow fleet ships sailing under false flags, report says
Detentions have helped cut the number of ships in Moscow's shadow fleet flying a false flag to less than half between last October and June 2026, according to a report by the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) think tank published on Sept. 25.
The Western crackdown against shadow vessels sailing under false flags has forced 107 to flock to the Russian flag registry since January 2025, leaving them with few other options as open ship registries tighten oversight.
The shadow fleet is a group of aging, poorly insured tankers used by Russia to ship out its oil in violation of international sanctions. Western governments have also accused Moscow of using the fleet to support its hybrid war against Europe.
European countries have become increasingly assertive in enforcing their sanctions against the fleet, with France, Sweden, Belgium, and the U.K. boarding suspected shadow fleet vessels that entered their territorial waters.
Shadow fleet ships have traditionally relied on open registries as they are cheap, lightly regulated, and make it easier to conceal the vessels' true ownership.
But countries running the open registries, such as Panama, Comoros, and others, have tightened oversight amid Western pressure.
"Following pressure from sanctioning jurisdictions, Barbados and Palau removed all sanctioned 'shadow' vessels from their registries, while Panama cut the number of sanctioned 'shadow' vessels in their registries by almost two-thirds since May 2025," the report read.
This has forced many shadow fleet vessels to sail under false flags, rendering them legally stateless and giving European countries grounds to detain them.
The most recent interception took place on Aug. 30 when an EU naval mission in the Mediterranean boarded the oil tanker MV Sun, suspected of belonging to the shadow fleet.
Following the crackdown, the number of shadow vessels flying false flags went from its peak of 101 in October 2025 to just 45 by the end of June, the CREA report read.
At the same time, the Russian ship registry surged by 36% since the start of last year to 382 by the end of June 2026.
Eighty-seven percent of the newly Russian-flagged vessels were already sanctioned, and 56% flew at least one false flag before being hit by sanctions and hoisting the Russian flag, according to the report.
Nevertheless, the pivot toward the Russian registry has slowed since the December 2025 peak, with only three new additions in June.
Adopting a Russian flag effectively makes the shadow fleet vessels immune to European interceptions and "renders obsolete the sanctions mechanism European navies have used to interdict them," CREA analysts say.

title: Así se usa ya la inteligencia artificial en clínicas y hospitales de España
content:
De tratamientos diarios para el TDAH infantil a transcripciones en la consulta: así se aplica ya la IA en clínicas y hospitales de España
Basado en hechos observados y verificados directamente por nuestros periodistas o por fuentes informadas.
Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google.
Dos empresas españolas exponen sus desarrollos durante la jornada 'La oportunidad de la IA para la salud', organizada por Google este miércoles.
La inteligencia artificial (IA) supone un cambio de paradigma en muchos campos de la vida. La salud no se queda fuera. En clínicas y hospitales del sector privado y público en España ya se están implementando soluciones desarrolladas con IA que buscan reducir la carga burocrática de los sanitarios para aumentar la atención de calidad a los pacientes. Sin embargo, la IA no va a sustituir al criterio médico ni va a tomar las decisiones que han de tomar los sanitarios, sino que les va a permitir "hacerlos mejores". Así lo han trasladado este miércoles varias voces especializadas durante la jornada organizada por Google en sus oficinas de Madrid bajo el título La oportunidad de la IA para la salud, durante la cual dos empresas han expuesto de primera mano sus experiencias e incipientes resultados.
En el campo de la salud mental, Ignacio de Ramón, CEO y cofundador de la startup Sincrolab (primero por la izquierda en la foto que encabeza esta información), ha explicado que su sistema basado en maching learning desarrolla tratamientos digitales para trastornos neuronales. Aterrizando: ha realizado una herramienta médica digital (aplicación) con la que niños con Trastorno por Déficit de Atención e Hiperactividad (TDAH) pueden realizar actividades y ejercicios cognitivos personalizados a diario. De esta forma, se incrementa el tratamiento y, por tanto, se acelera y reduce el tiempo necesario porque "aumenta la eficacia".
"En salud mental es prácticamente inviable realizar intervenciones todos los días, nosotros ofrecemos un tratamiento adecuado todos los días. En salud mental, los profesionales adaptan los tratamientos cuando los pacientes aparecen en consulta. Nosotros lo queremos hacer todos los días para reducir el tiempo de los tratamientos, para aumentar la eficacia de los tratamientos aumentando la dosis", ha expuesta De Ramón.
Su empresa, una de las tres españolas seleccionadas en el programa programa Growth Academy: AI for Health de 'Google for Startups', comenzó en 2015 y desde entonces ha estado desarrollando ensayos clínicos de las aplicaciones que ya llegan a los pacientes, de momento pediátricos y en breve también adultos, y cuyos resultados pueden monitorear a diario los facultativos. Además, están investigando otras aplicaciones para tratar el deterioro cognitivo del ictus y prevenir la demencia. Sus clientes son, hasta el momento, "casi cien clínicas, la gran mayoría privadas, y estamos pilotando en varios hospitales".
"La idea es que los niños mejoren sus capacidades cognitivas a través del juego. Son tareas y actividades arduas a nivel cognitivo y es totalmente diferente a lo que necesita un paciente adulto de TDAH. Cada tratamiento y aplicación se adapta al lenguaje de los pacientes, adapta los componentes y, en función de cómo está rindiendo, sube o baja el nivel para maximizar el rendimiento", ha explicado De Ramón.
Con su terapia digital para TDAH (trastorno que afecta a una de cada 15 personas en todo el mundo, según diversos estudios), al menos 3 de cada 4 pacientes (75%) mostraron una mejora relevante en impulsividad, y cerca de 2 de cada 3 (66%) mostraron una mejora relevante en los síntomas cotidianos, según los datos expuestos este miércoles durante la mesa redonda. La empresa está
"El médico tiene su entrevista con el paciente, le pregunta, le escucha, pero no tiene que estar picando en el ordenador"
Próximamente tienen previsto lanzar una herramienta que utiliza "pacientes artificiales" para que psicólogos y psiquiatras puedan practicar habilidades de entrevista, diagnóstico y tratamiento de problemas como depresión, ansiedad o trastornos de la conducta alimentaria (TCA).
Con todo, De Ramón ha asegurado que "todavía queda bastante para cambiar las reglas de todo el juego". En el sistema británico de salud (NHS, por sus siglas en inglés), tras 20 años introduciendo tratamientos digitales en salud mental, estos siguen por debajo de las prescripciones de biblioterapia (con cuadernos para realizar anotaciones), ha apuntado el fundador de Sincrolab.
Un "copiloto médico" que ahorra trabajo
Por su parte, la responsable de regulación de Omniloy, Nuria Pérez, ha explicado que su empresa desarrolla herramientas de IA que automatizan procesos de atención médica. Según ha explicado a 20minutos, han desarrollado un agente de IA que agiliza procesos iniciales de citaciones "que quitan un poco la parte burocrática" hasta que te derivan a especialidades.
Otro de sus productos es un "copiloto médico", es decir, una herramienta informática con IA que realiza las funciones de un "asistente de consulta" que "va grabando, tomando notas y transcribe toda la consulta que has tenido con el paciente, de tal manera que luego proporciona un código CIE-10 [Clasificación Internacional de Enfermedades], e incluso te ofrece recomendaciones de por dónde tienes que ir".
"El médico tiene su entrevista con el paciente, le pregunta, le escucha, pero no tiene que estar picando todo el rato en el ordenador. De esa forma te aseguras que los datos del historial son los que de verdad el paciente dice, mientras que el médico puede centrarse en hacer las preguntas para realizar el diagnóstico, y no tiene que perder tiempo". Según explica la portavoz de la empresa, a través de esta herramienta se consigue una transcripción de la conversación en consulta que queda recogida en el ordenador del médico a través del micrófono del mismo, lo cual permite al sanitario centrarse en la atención del paciente. "Ahora estamos trabajando en nuevos productos más enfocados al triaje, al seguimiento y a la prevención", agrega.
Los clientes de Omniloy, creada hace un año y medio también reconocida por Google, son HM Hospitales y 16 centros de Atención Primaria de la Comunidad Valenciana y Cataluña, entre otros. Esta empresa es uno de los cinco proveedores del Ministerio de Sanidad de España para la digitalización de hospitales ."Nuestro foco es el personal sanitario y la seguridad de los pacientes, mejorar la atención de los pacientes y hacerla más humana". La agocida, asegura, es "muy buena porque estamos reduciendo la carga administrativa y dejando a los sanitarios más tiempo para atender a sus pacientes".
"No creo que la IA vaya a sustituir a los médicos sino que va a hacerlos mejores, no solo por tener más tiempo sin para abarcar más datos para preguntas más complejas"
Según ha expuesto Marina Santaciles, responsable del programa Google Research y encagada de conducir la mesa redonda, el agente de IA desarrollado por Omniloy ha demostrado un 92% de precisión, superando la del trabajo manual. Pérez ha señalado que estos datos están generando "confianza" tanto en pacientes como en el personal sanitarios. Desde la empresa, aseguran que aspiran a convertirse en el "cerebro del hospital", es decir, "una segunda capa que trabaja 24/7 por debajo de todo la infraestructura sanitaria", pero "teniendo siempre el foco de que el médico es el que decide".
En el debate también ha intervenido el doctor Pablo Velasco Puyó, oncólogo pediátrico del Hospital Universitario Vall d'Hebron de Barcelona, y miembro de la iniciativa Capricorn, dedicada a analizar literatura y datos biomédicos con modelos de IA Google Gemini para identificar opciones de tratamiento personalizado contra el cáncer infantil. En su opinión, la IA "permite ganar tiempo para dedicárselo a los pacientes y para innovar".
Tras asegurar que no ve límites a la IA, ha señalado que el reto actual no es tanto tecnológico sino la validación de proyectos, tanto externa como a nivel prospectivo. "Necesitamos juntarnos la academia y los clínicos para tener un impacto real y asegurarnos de que disminuimos al máximo el riesgo en los pacientes", ha defendido. "No creo que la IA vaya a sustituir a los médicos sino que va a hacerlos mejores, no solo por tener más tiempo sin para abarcar más datos para preguntas más complejas", ha añadido.

title: Lauren Sanchez, Bezos pour $25M into Pacific project
content:
Listen to this article in summarized format
Lauren Sanchez is highlighting a major new ocean conservation effort backed by the Bezos Earth Fund, as the organization founded by Jeff Bezos commits more than $25 million to protect and sustainably manage waters across five Pacific nations. The latest funding will support conservation projects in the Cook Islands, Kiribati, Papua New Guinea, Tonga and Vanuatu, covering more than 625,000 square miles of ocean — an area larger than Alaska.
The new grants are part of the Bezos Earth Fund's broader $100 million commitment to Pacific-led ocean conservation and will also help governments develop proposals for protecting international waters under the UN High Seas Treaty.
ALSO READ: Sam Altman was just 19 when he left Stanford to build an app Loopt that struggled to take off; years before ChatGPT, Green Dot paid $43.4 million for it
Lauren Sanchez connects Pacific experience to new ocean funding
Lauren Sanchez, vice chair of the Bezos Earth Fund, pointed to her own recent experience in the Pacific while discussing why protecting the region's oceans matters. In July, Sanchez shared photos and videos from a snorkeling and scuba-diving trip in Fiji, where she saw reefs surrounded by fish, sea turtles and reef sharks.Her experience also gave her a closer look at the connection between healthy oceans and the communities that depend on them. In an Instagram video announcing the latest funding, Sanchez emphasized that Pacific communities have protected and cared for their waters for generations.
The new grants are designed to support those locally led conservation efforts rather than replace them.
ALSO READ: Canada man spent 32 years searching for answers. When his daughter developed similar symptoms, one Google search changed everything
Bezos Earth Fund expands ocean conservation across five Pacific nations
The more than $25 million in new grants will fund different conservation priorities in each of the five countries.In the Cook Islands, BirdLife International will help expand protections through the Marae Moana framework. The whole-of-ocean marine park already covers more than 734,000 square miles.
In Kiribati, Live & Learn Environmental Education will work on identifying important marine habitats, improving monitoring and enforcement, and advancing legal protection for priority areas.
Papua New Guinea will receive support from the Wildlife Conservation Society as the country works toward establishing its first large offshore marine protected area.
In Tonga, TierraMar will support the creation of new protected areas as the country works toward its goal of protecting 30% of its ocean.
And in Vanuatu, Live & Learn will help put the country's completed national marine spatial plan into action, including offshore conservation areas and community-led marine management.
Lauren Sanchez's involvement also puts a public face on the Bezos Earth Fund's latest conservation push
New effort also focuses on international waters
The Bezos Earth Fund's latest investment goes beyond the waters controlled by individual Pacific nations.A separate grant to Rare will bring Pacific governments together to develop some of the region's first marine protected area proposals for international waters under the UN High Seas Treaty.
The treaty entered into force in January 2026, creating a framework for protecting biodiversity in areas of the ocean beyond national jurisdiction.
That matters for marine animals that do not stay within one country's borders.
Whales, sharks, sea turtles and tuna can travel across vast stretches of the Pacific, moving between national waters and the high seas.
Conservation efforts therefore need to extend beyond individual marine protected areas if countries want to protect species throughout their migration routes.
Funding will support monitoring and local communities
The latest grants are not focused only on creating new protected areas. The money will also support monitoring, enforcement, community stewardship and long-term financing.That is important because designating an area as protected does not automatically guarantee that conservation rules will be followed.
Effective management can require continued monitoring, enforcement resources and cooperation with communities that rely on the ocean for food, employment and other parts of their livelihoods.
The Bezos Earth Fund says the broader Pacific initiative is intended to help countries develop conservation systems that can continue beyond the initial creation of protected areas.
Bezos Earth Fund has now committed $63.3 million
The latest grants bring the Bezos Earth Fund's total commitments under its $100 million Pacific initiative to $63.3 million.The first round of funding, announced in 2025, provided $37.5 million through seven grants.
The organization has also supported conservation work in other Pacific locations, including French Polynesia and Niue.
Earlier this year, French Polynesia established what was described as the world's largest network of fully protected marine areas, covering nearly 625,000 square miles of ocean.
In Niue, about 40% of the country's national waters are already protected.
With the second round of Bezos Earth Fund funding, 17 of the Pacific's 22 countries and territories are now working on efforts to protect or sustainably manage their waters.
Why Pacific ocean protection matters
The Pacific is home to extensive coral reefs, marine habitats and migratory species, while coastal communities depend heavily on healthy ocean ecosystems.That makes conservation a particularly regional issue.
A protected area created by one country may safeguard part of a species' habitat, but animals that travel hundreds or thousands of miles can still encounter threats outside those boundaries.
The new initiative therefore combines national conservation efforts with plans for protecting biodiversity in international waters.
Lauren Sanchez's involvement also puts a public face on the Bezos Earth Fund's latest conservation push, with her recent Pacific experience providing a personal connection to the region's marine ecosystems.
The fund's latest commitment represents another step toward its larger $100 million Pacific conservation goal, with more than $63 million now committed.
For the five countries receiving the latest grants, the funding will support different priorities — from new marine protected areas and habitat monitoring to enforcement, community stewardship and preparations for conservation proposals covering international waters.

title: Iranian rower trained through bombing raids to win Asian Games gold
content:
Kimia Zarei was preparing for the Asian Games when the sound of bombs became part of her training routine.
She would get ready to work out at home, hear an explosion nearby and look out of the window to see smoke rising. Then she would return to her ergometer and carry on rowing.
For 45 days, that was how Zarei and the rest of Iran’s rowing team prepared for the Asian Games, separately, inside their homes, in cities spread across a country at war. “The only thing that we could do was take one ergometer and take it home,” said Zarei, who paired with Zeinab Norouzi to win gold in the women’s lightweight double sculls. “Every day, try to row, try to have training sessions on erg, and connect with our coach, get the training schedule, and row on erg.”




The war had begun six months before the Games, catching the athletes unprepared. On its first day, the federation cancelled its training camp and sent the rowers back to their homes. “We faced a lot of difficulties after the war began, but we wanted to show that we are strong. We have given every rower an ergometer so they could continue training at home,” said Iran’s rowing federation chief Mohsen Shadi Naghadeh.
Zarei returned to Hamadan. Her teammates went back to their own cities.
The conflict began in February, following large-scale attacks by the United States and Israel, and disrupted sporting preparations across Iran. For the rowers, there was little choice but to find a way to train around it. “All the cities in Iran were affected by the war,” Zarei said. “In the first month of the war, it was really hard, harder than before.”
Click here to read our Asian Games full coverage
There were interruptions. Sometimes they had to leave home when the bombing intensified. Sometimes they had to stop what they were doing and move somewhere else. But the training continued. “It was both of them,” Zarei said, when asked whether, in those first weeks, she was trying to save her life or trying to row.
Story continues below this ad
The rowing team was not alone in trying to salvage an Asian Games preparation thrown into chaos. Iran’s women’s kabaddi team also had its camp disrupted by the war and had to move between cities before travelling to Sonepat in India in August, where the players trained twice a day and played practice matches to regain the rhythm lost during the conflict.
For Zarei, those first 45 days were spent almost entirely indoors. She estimates she covered about 20 kilometres a day on the ergometer, alone in her room, following a training schedule sent by her coach. “I was preparing to start training, and then I heard the bombing sounds,” she said. “It was so close to our home. When you looked out of the window, you could see the smoke.”
…
Eventually, the team was able to return to camp and resume rowing on water. Zarei trained in Urmia, where Iran’s rowing federation had access to a two-kilometre course. The uncertainty of those 45 days did not disappear when she returned to the water. Another memory was waiting for her.
At the Hangzhou Asian Games three years ago, she had finished fourth, the only member of Iran’s rowing team to leave without a medal. “It was really a hard moment,” she said.
Story continues below this ad
That fourth-place finish continues to rankle her, and so do the three years that followed: the training, the effort to stay positive, the belief that she could do better. “Three years of hard work, being motivated, trying to stay positive, trying to believe in myself and believing in God,” she said. “Today, I’ve got first place.”
As she crossed the finish line in Nagoya, the emotion of those three years, and of those weeks in Iran, came out. Zarei splashed the water and broke down.
Throughout the war, she had kept returning to the same thought. “The only thing was thinking about the medal, thinking about my people, thinking about my family and my future,” she said. “Because this medal really matters for Iranian people, especially Iranian girls.” Then the tears. “I cried,” she said. “It was a moment that I really cannot explain in words.”



For 45 days, Zarei had trained without a boat, without teammates beside her, with the sound of bombing sometimes breaking into her sessions. “I told myself, I will do my best. I will have training every day. Please help me to get the best result.”
It was gold.

title: A Causal Multi-modal AI Model Stratifies Residual Risk and Identifies Candidates for Treatment Escalation in Node-Positive HR+/HER2- Early Breast Cancer
content: PURPOSE Prognostic biomarkers that estimate residual recurrence risk after standard adjuvant therapy to guide further treatment escalation are an unmet clinical need. This study used Ataraxis Breast CTX, a causal multi-modal AI model integrating clinical variables and histopathology, to stratify residual risk in clinically defined high-risk patients. We aimed to identify patients who have excellent outcomes on standard-of-care chemoendocrine therapy and patients who may benefit from additional therapies such as everolimus or CDK4/6 inhibitors. METHODS CTX combines clinical variables with image features from H&E images to produce estimates of recurrence risk (CTX-prognostic) and chemotherapy benefit (CTX-benefit). Prospective-retrospective validation was performed in the phase III UNIRAD trial to assess CTX-prognostic's performance in the subset of patients who had not received neoadjuvant chemotherapy, who had received adjuvant chemotherapy, and who had H&E slides available (n = 556). The primary endpoint in this study was disease-free survival (DFS). As an exploratory analysis, we evaluated CTX-benefit's ability to predict benefit from adjuvant everolimus. RESULTS CTX-prognostic effectively stratified patients into high- and low-risk groups. Across all patients, 5-year DFS was significantly higher in the low-risk group (93%) than in the high-risk group (80%). Additionally, treatment benefit from everolimus differed significantly by CTX-benefit score in an exploratory multivariable analysis adjusting for age, tumor size, nodal status, grade, and menopausal status (interaction p = 0.01). CONCLUSION CTX identified patients with good outcomes under chemoendocrine therapy alone and patients with residual risk who may benefit from treatment escalation. Additionally, CTX was found to be predictive of everolimus benefit. These results suggest that CTX may effectively stratify clinically high-risk HR+/HER2- patients by residual risk and may inform selection of adjuvant escalation strategies.

title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 5931: Nested Spatiotemporal Anomaly Detection with Semantic Augmentation: A Case Study in Heritage Conservation
content: Cultural heritage (CH) sites are continuously exposed to pressures that can lead to deterioration. Continuous monitoring and anomaly detection (AD) enable early damage detection for preventive conservation. We propose a late-fusion AD framework combining NST-Net, a nested spatiotemporal neural network, with a semantic module encoding expert conservation rules, and evaluate it on five real-world CH monitoring datasets. NST-Net outperforms six state-of-the-art baselines on most sites, achieving, on average, 42% higher Average Precision than the best baseline per site under a synthetic evaluation protocol emphasizing sharp, short-duration anomalies. Dataset length serves as an important performance factor: the combined architecture and preprocessing pipeline particularly benefit longer campaigns, whereas they add little value on shorter ones. NST-Net also requires approximately 13 times less peak memory than baseline detectors, at a higher but still millisecond-scale latency. Further analysis shows that performance depends strongly on anomaly density, type, and severity. The semantic module passes label-free sanity checks and complements NST-Net effectively (complementarity index > 0.87), identifying conservation-relevant events missed by the deep model. These findings support late-fusion statistical–semantic frameworks for AD in CH monitoring.

title: ABC sterilisation, anti-rabies vaccination drives intensified in Thoothukudi; 408 dogs sterilised, 3,163 vaccinated in eight months
content:
In the last eight months, Thoothukudi Corporation has sterilised 408 stray dogs under the Animal Birth Control (ABC) programme and administered Anti-Rabies Vaccination (ARV) to 3,163 stray dogs.
According to an official from Thoothukudi Corporation, earlier the Corporation has carried out ABC programme for stray dogs with the assistance of Animal Husbandry Department and Tamil Nadu Animal Welfare Board (TNAWB) at the veterinary dispensary at Pudukottai. Following that, the dogs were kept under observation at the shelter at the Corporation’s Tharuvaikulam dumping yard before being released.
However in July, he added that the Corporation has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the a NGO called RAIN (Rescuing Animals in Need), and the ABC sterilisation began at a renovated shed at the Corporation’s dumping yard which comprises an operation theater and kennel.
The official added after the entry of NGO into the sterilisation programme, 60 to 80 stray dogs per week were being sterilised and administered with ARV, and the programme was being implemented in a phased manner.
Mentioning that stray dogs in the streets and public spaces of Thoothukudi Corporation were earlier administered with ARV though dedicated drive once a week, he said the vaccination drive was now conducted everyday based on the complaints from the public. He said the plans were also under way to register the number of dogs sterilised under ABC on the TNAWB portal and Bharat Pashudhan Portal.
The official further stated the number of stray dogs sterilised under the ABC programme had increased significantly over the past two months compared with previous months.
Speaking to The Hindu, Thoothukudi Corporation Commissioner S. Priyanka said that along with ABC sterilisation ARV drive has also been intensified within the Corporation limits. She added that the Corporation was constructing another ABC centre at Muthiahpuram and animal shelter at Tharuvaikulam dumping yard, to ensure regular monitoring and control of the stray dog population in the city. She also urged the residents to feed the stray dogs only at 36 designated feeding points in the city to help control the stray dog population.

title: Las plataneras vuelven a abrirse camino sobre la lava del volcán de La Palma: "Tuve que usar un GPS para encontrar mi parcela"
content:
Las plataneras vuelven a abrirse camino sobre la lava del volcán de La Palma: "Tuve que usar un GPS para encontrar mi parcela"
Basado en hechos observados y verificados directamente por nuestros periodistas o por fuentes informadas.
Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google.
Más de un tercio de los cultivos arrasados por el volcán han sido ya reconstruidos sobre la colada, aunque la falta de carreteras sigue entorpeciendo el proceso.
La carretera se abre camino por el mar de piedra volcánica, los restos de la erupción que durante tres meses expulsó el volcán del Tajogaite en la isla de La Palma. Han pasado cinco años, y este territorio que fue un manto verde de plataneras es ahora un desierto negro. Pero de tanto en tanto, siempre junto a la carretera, las fincas están empezando a brotar y la agricultura se vuelve a abrir camino en la parte baja del Valle de Aridane.
"Todo esto lo cubrió la lava, todo, todo. Solo dejó esas montañas que ves ahí", declara César González, un agricultor palmero de 50 años, antiguo vecino del desaparecido pueblo de Todoque donde perdió su vivienda y, a medida que la lava iba descendiendo por la ladera de Cumbre Vieja, también sus cultivos. Ahora habla desde el mismo lugar donde se ubicaban sus plataneras, aunque la orografía es ahora totalmente distinta. Él tuvo la suerte de que una de las dos carreteras que se abrieron para atravesar la colada, pasaba justo por donde estaba su terreno.
"Hicieron primero la carretera de arriba, pero quizás al año ya estaba esta", declara señalando la vía que flanquea su parcela. "La primera vez que entré con la camioneta cuando no estaba ni asfaltada, cogí el móvil, más o menos con el GPS y me fui orientando. Sin móvil no llegas, no sabes ni dónde estás, porque no tienes referencias. Y llegué y dije: 'Contra, pues yo creo que si de lo más alto quito para lo más bajo, se nivela. Vamos a ver cómo van, cómo van saliendo las ayudas y me pongo a ello".
La lava destruyó 288 hectáreas de plataneras en 2021, que representaban entonces más del 10% de la economía de La Palma de forma directa y el 43% de toda la superficie agrícola de La Palma. Quedaron sepultadas bajo el volcán 14.000 toneladas de plátanos, según datos de la Asociación Palmera de Agricultores y Ganaderos (Aspa) una décima parte de la producción actual -cifrada en 140.000 toneladas por el Instituto Canario de Estadística en 2024-, que aún no ha alcanzado los volúmenes previos a la erupción.
La recuperación está siendo lenta, pero firme. En abril de este año, la Asociación de Entidades Empaquetadoras, Exportadoras y Comercializadoras de Frutos de La Palma (Asepalma) calculaba que un 37% de las hectáreas que habían sido devastadas por el volcán estaban ya en marcha en el Valle de Aridane. La Consejería de Agricultura canaria estimó unas cifras muy similares.
"Cuando el plátano tose, La Palma se resfría"
Los plataneros han recibido distintos paquetes de ayudas millonarias procedentes del Gobierno de Canarias, del Estado central y de la Unión Europea tanto para compensar la pérdida de renta como para reconstruir las fincas desde 2021. El Gobierno canario compensó la reconstrucción de las explotaciones con 44,06 euros por cada metro cuadrado perdido durante la erupción a cada agricultor.
A pesar de toda esa inyección económica, cinco años después las propias administraciones y el sector siguen calculando en cientos de millones el coste pendiente de reconstrucción. En febrero de 2026, Gobierno de Canarias y Asepalma calculaban que todavía faltaban 224 millones de euros para completar la reconstrucción agraria del Valle de Aridane: 56,4 millones para las explotaciones, 68,8 millones para caminos y 82,2 millones para agua, además de 11,5 millones para producción.
"La importancia económica es que cuando el plátano está bien, la economía insular está bien y cuando el plátano tose, todo el mundo tiene un resfriado", declara Miguel Martín Pérez, presidente de la Asociación Palmera de Agricultores y Ganaderos (Aspa), que lamenta que los retrasos en la llegada de las ayudas han hecho que la inflación de los precios haga insuficientes las cuantías recibidas por los agricultores.
"Con ese dinero en este momento no da para reconstruir ¿Por qué? Porque es más caro. Porque han subido los precios, porque hay una oferta y una demanda, porque no hay suelo. Es decir, por una serie de circunstancias, ahora es más caro", explica Martín Pérez. "Esos 224 millones de euros quizás puedan faltar para poder reconstruir todo, pues, digamos: 'Oiga, van a venir este año tantos, van a venir el año próximo tantos. Usted va a tener tres o cuatro años para hacer ese proceso'. Y a partir de esa fecha, deberíamos estar todos con esa producción otra vez nueva. Lo que nos gustaría es que el manto negro pase a ser verde de plátano, como era antes de la erupción".
Volver a abrir vías por la colada
Sobre el terreno, César señala al gran obstáculo para que la negra colada se vaya tornando de nuevo en verde. "Yo conozco varios amigos míos que quieren retomar su cultivo. ¿Cuál es el problema? Que no tienen el acceso. Es lo que falta a la gente, son los accesos. Sin acceso no te dan la licencia, no te lo permiten, y ¿cómo llegas? Él quiere, él tiene el dinero, tiene la voluntad, pero ¿y cómo llego yo ahí?", se pregunta el agricultor.
A su espalda, dentro del invernadero, una excavadora realiza los últimos preparativos sobre la tierra traída ex profeso desde Los Llanos y alojada sobre la piedra volcánica para hacer posible el cultivo de las plataneras. A final de mes, espera estar cultivando, pero a su alrededor, casi todo sigue siendo colada de lava.
"Para poder recuperar totalmente las fincas que se perdieron, eso implica, evidentemente, abrir los caminos que llegan a las fincas. Y poner el agua. Hay que pensar que una finca con tierra sin agua no es nada, es un terreno baldío", declara Javier Llamas, alcalde de Los Llanos de Aridane, el municipio que perdió la mayor cantidad de hectáreas cultivadas en el valle y que mantiene lo que él denomina su "guerra contra el Estado" para recibir las ayudas que se ajusten a toda la infraestructura perdida durante la erupción que debe ser ahora reconstruida. "Yo no no pretendo que me manden el dinero de golpe. Yo lo que quiero es que hagamos una hoja de ruta. Soy el municipio peor parado. Mi reconstrucción se va a parar si no cuento con el Estado. Yo no tengo 66 millones de euros. No tengo ni la mitad".
César se muestra optimista sobre cuándo podrá reactivar su producción. Para su finca, solo falta completar las zanjas y la instalación del riego por aspersión, gestionado por una comunidad de regantes. Una vez que tenga agua, planea sembrar a finales de septiembre o principios de octubre, esperando que la producción comience en 10-12 meses, y la cosecha en 3-4 meses adicionales. Cree que pronto sus vecinos seguirán su ejemplo y el de otros y el paisaje volcánico irá recuperando su antigua apariencia.
"Yo creo que poco a poco le damos un susto a todo esto. Cuando se empezó en todo esto por aquí, éramos dos, tal vez tres. Este fue el primero que hizo. El resto, nadie quería hacer nada. De hecho yo tengo un familiar que en su momento le dije que yo iba a empezar y me dijo que no lo veía y cuando vino a vérmela dijo: 'Contra, Dios, pues mira, no pensaba…'. Él no pensaba que era posible. Pues ahora ya está haciéndola la de él", declara César, que ya ha reconstruido también su vivienda, aunque no en Todoque, de momento.
—¿Se puede decir que ya casi estás a punto de superar la crisis del volcán?
—"En mi caso… sí. Lo principal sí, yo creo que sí".

title: Six years without stubble burning: Barnala brothers’ 3-crop model on 105 acres

For farmer brothers Sukhpal Singh Jawandha and Tarsem Singh Jawandha of Kothe Surjitpura village in Punjab’s Barnala district, stubble management has gone hand in hand with crop diversification and better farm returns.
The brothers cultivate around 105 acres and grow potatoes on nearly 80-85 acres, supplying their produce to Haldiram and other food-processing firms. For the past six years, they have also avoided burning paddy stubble, instead incorporating it into the soil.
After harvesting paddy, Sukhpal Singh Jawandha, 43, son of Mewa Singh Jawandha, and his brother Tarsem Singh Jawandha, 46, plant potatoes on about 80-85 acres and wheat on about 20 acres. After digging out the potatoes, we sow maize on about 40 acres. In addition, we also cultivate moong and watermelon.”
The brothers follow a crop cycle that allows them to take three crops in a year, thereby promoting crop diversification.
Sukhpal said they had been managing paddy stubble for around six years. “We have been managing stubble for about six years. We harvest paddy with a Super SMS(Straw Management System)-equipped combine. After that, we mix the stubble into the soil (mulching). Following this, we plough the field and run a rotavator before sowing potatoes,” he said.
The practice has also evolved over the years. “Before 2024, we used to make bales of stubble, but now we do mulching. The potato yield was around 250 to 300 bags (each bag containing 50 kg), which has now increased to 350 bags per acre,” he said.
The farmers were provided with a subsidised Super Seeder by the government, while they purchased an MB plough and rotavator themselves in 2024. They use the Super Seeder for sowing wheat.
‘Farmers need more subsidised machinery’
Sukhpal said they had not faced any difficulty after adopting stubble-management practices and claimed that both crop yield and profits had increased. He also said farmers needed access to more machinery on subsidy to make residue management easier and reduce financial burden.
The brothers own around 21 acres, while the remaining land is on lease. “Even after meeting the expenses, we save around Rs 40,000 per acre annually,” they said. This works out to an annual income of Rs 42 lakh after covering all expenses.
The farmers said marketing their potato crop had never been a problem. “We supply potatoes to Haldiram and other such firms for food processing. We have never faced any problem in marketing the potatoes and get good prices,” Sukhpal said.
Sukhpal said there was good demand for stubble this year and that a large number of balers were available in the district. Appealing to farmers not to burn paddy residue, he said, “Burning stubble kills beneficial insects in the soil and also adversely affects human health, animals, and the environment.”
Barnala Deputy Commissioner Harpreet Singh lauded the Jawandha brothers for managing stubble while simultaneously promoting crop diversification.
“Under the stubble management campaign, the Barnala district administration is not only creating awareness among farmers but is also mapping machinery, including balers and pellet units, village-wise so that farmers do not face any difficulty. I urge farmers to take full advantage of government schemes,” he said.
The deputy commissioner appealed to farmers across the district to adopt eco-friendly techniques for managing paddy residue.

title: Family shares hidden cost of cancer care
content:
Family shares hidden cost of cancer care
- Published
The parents of a teenage girl with a rare form of childhood cancer say the hidden costs of caring for their daughter have left them in fear of losing their home.
Maya, 13, from Hythe in Kent, was diagnosed with neuroblastoma at three years old, but relapsed in 2023 having been in remission for five years.
Her mother, Dellanie, said the pressure of paying a mortgage and bills whilst she and her husband, Terry, are working less to care for Maya is continuing to take its toll on their family of five.
Dellanie, an NHS nurse, said: "Whilst your child is poorly and you are fighting for her life, the bills don't stop coming."
She added: "My husband has lost his income as he is caring for Maya, and these days you need two people working just to keep your head above water.
"It has been very, very difficult but our aim has always been to to look after our child as well as each other.
"I always put a brave face on - of course I'm hurting, but I can't be in the corner crying."
Maya, who her mother described as a "larger than life person" who loves animals and music, was first diagnosed with neuroblastoma near her adrenal gland when she was three-years-old.
Neuroblastoma is a rare cancer which mainly affects children under five-years-old and around 100 children are diagnosed with it a year in the UK, according to Cancer Research UK.
After initially going into remission, Maya's neuroblastoma returned three years ago, and has since been cared for by specialist teams including at the Royal Marsden hospital in London, and Great Ormond Street Hospital.
In 2025, during a clinical trial of CAR T-cell therapy, a technique currently used to treat some types of leukaemia and lymphoma, Maya developed a brain injury which Dellanie said left her "profoundly disabled".
Her disability meant Terry had to leave his job to care for Maya full time, while Dellanie reduced her working hours to care for her, and support her husband.
Dellanie said: "I just have to be grateful for what we have got.
"At the moment, Maya is a fighter and there is so much fight in her."
'Thrown into chaos'
Charity Young Lives vs Cancer says families of children with cancer face average extra costs of around £700 a month, and an average loss of income of about £6,000 per household.
Sonia Malik, the charity's associate policy director, said: "We find people are having to dip into savings, and most of these costs are immediate.
"It impacts the whole family and their lives are thrown into chaos.
"The financial stress should be the last thing families have to think about."
Malik said that some support is available for cancer patients and their carers, such as financial support from charities, disability benefits and carer's allowance, but it can take time for families to receive benefits support.

title: Stray cat Lottie produces unusual litter of nine
content:
Stray cat Lottie produces unusual litter of nine
- Published
A rescue cat has given birth to nine kittens - one of the biggest litters the RSPCA's Bridlington branch has seen in years.
Three-year-old Lottie and her offspring - five males and four females - are being cared for at a cattery run by the RSPCA's Bridlington, Driffield and District Branch.
Typically, a cat has four to six kitten in a single litter, according to the RSPCA.
Cattery manager Sophie Gibbon-Roles said: "For now, Lottie's whole world is these nine little faces and we're helping her to keep them warm, clean, fed and safe."
Lottie, who was not microchipped or wearing a collar, was found wandering in Wold Newton a few weeks ago by a member of the public.
Gibbon-Roles described Lottie as "one incredibly brave and devoted mum".
As the five-week-old litter is so large, the branch is helping Lottie by syringe-feeding the kittens twice a day.
"It's incredible watching them grow and seeing their different personalities start to come through," Gibbon-Roles added.
The Bridlington branch has cared for 127 cats and kittens so far this year - a 41% increase compared to the same time last year.
It said rising numbers are due to people are not prioritising neutering. The branch also warned overbreeding could lead to more kittens being born with infections.
Gibbon-Roles said: "It's been an exceptionally busy year for cats and kittens. It's been a juggling act from the get-go.
"As soon as one cattery space becomes available, it gets filled up immediately."
She added: "Every unwanted litter adds to the growing number of cats needing homes, placing more pressure on already overwhelmed rescues.
"Neutering isn't just about stopping unwanted kittens, it's about preventing a cycle that can lead to suffering."
Donations of kitten milk and mousse are requested to help feed the litter.
